FAMILY WELFARE
 
I           INTRODUCTION
 
1.1   India, the largest democratic republic in the world possesses 2.4% of the world’s land area and supports 16% of the
world population. In terms of population growth rate, there has been decline during the decade 1991-2001 as compared
to previous decade 1981-1991, due to the prolonged Family Planning Campaign. According to world population
projections by the United Nations, it is estimated that India would have a population of 1533 million by the year 2050
and in that year it will surpass China, currently the most populous country in the world.
1.2       Since 1951, the year India’s Family Planning programme was launched; its demographic and health profiles
have changed radically. Between 1951 and 2002, Crude Birth Rate (CBR) has declined from 40.8 to 25.0 per thousand
population and Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) from an average of 146 to 63 per thousand live births during the same
period. The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) has also come down from 437 in 1992-93 as per NFHS-I to 407 in 1998
(as per SRS) per 100,000 live births. Significant improvement is also there in the Immunization Coverage.
1.3       Committee observes that there have been significant changes in the demographic and health profile of the
country. The Committee would, however, like to point out that average rate of various health indicators does not
indicate the ground realities in the big and populous states of the country. The Committee notes that
performance level in such states continues to remain much below the average national rate. A few examples as
indicated below are self-revealing:-

1.4       Committee’s attention has been drawn by a recent World Bank study, ‘Country Strategy for India - September,
2004’ which has mentioned that based on the existing data, the Maternal Mortality Rate has worsened. The Committee
notes that the National Family Health Survey-I (NFHS-I), 1991-92 estimated the Maternal Mortality Rate at 424 per
100,000 live births. However, NFHS-II , 1997-1998 estimated the MMR as 540 per 100,000 live births. It has also been
mentioned in the World Bank study, that there are problems with the data for this indicator in some of the largest states
that raise questions regarding data at the national level. The report of the NFHS-II also acknowledges that the difference
in the estimates of MMR of NFHS-I and NFHS-II is not statistically significant due to various reasons such as large
sampling errors etc.
1.5     Committee is not fully convinced by the contention of the Department that SRS, RGI have estimated the MMR
for the country as 407 per 100,000 live births in 1998 which is the same period when NFHS-II have estimated the NMR
as 540 per 100,000 live births. The fact remains that there are some problem areas in data collection. Non-availability of
reliable estimates of maternal mortality has been admitted by the Department also in its Annual Report (2004-05).   The
Committee notes that an expert group has been constituted in the Department which is looking into the modalities of
carrying out a survey for collection of data on Maternal Mortality.  A Pilot survey for this has already been completed.
Similar problems may be there in respect of other health indicators also. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that
the Department should carry out a comparative analysis of findings of NFHS-I and NFHS-II in order to understand the
factors responsible for discrepancies in the two Survey Reports. The Committee would also like to emphasise that the
entire Family Welfare planning is based on the National Surveys being conducted at regular intervals. Therefore, it
should be ensured that accurate data is made the basis of all health surveys. This can be achieved to a large extent by
monitoring of data being obtained specially from the states not performing well by involving Central teams also in the
collection of data, to the extent possible.
II         TENTH FIVE  YEAR  PLAN-MID TERM APPRAISAL
2.1       The Tenth Plan has specified the following monitorable targets to be achieved by the end of the Plan i.e. 2007.
1.
                  Reduction in decadal rate of population growth between 2001-2011 to 16.2%.
2.                  Reduction in Infant Mortality Rate to 45 per thousand live births by 2007.
3.                  Reduction in Maternal Mortality Rate to 2 per 1000 live births by 2007.
2.2       The other targets sought to be achieved by the end of the Plan are Total Fertility Rate of 2.3, Crude Birth Rate of
21, 100% coverage of children under immunization against six vaccines preventable diseases, 90% coverage of pregnant
women under three Antenatal check-ups and 100% coverage of pregnant women under 2 doses of TT & supply of IFA
tablets, ensuring 80% deliveries through health care institutions and 100% deliveries to be attended by trained health
personnel.

corresponding achievements as per latest estimates available are as under:

2.5       The Committee is constrained to observe that the expected levels of some of the indicators by the terminal year
of the Tenth Plan are very high when compared with the actual achievement level reached by the end of Ninth Plan, i.e
2002.   The Committee feels that the percentage of performance reached at the end of the Ninth Plan was virtually the
same in respect of these indicators. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the immediate goal of the
Department/State Govt./implementing agencies should be put to a sustained exercise in motion where under the weakest
performing districts (state-wise) are identified and targeted interventions are initiated, accompanied by regular
monitoring.    
III        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
3.1       Against an approved outlay of Rs. 15120 crores for the Department in Ninth Plan, funds made available were
only Rs. 14968.70 crores. This was further reduced to Rs. 14102.38 crores at the RE stage. Actual expenditure was only
Rs. 13968.72 crores. The Committee feels that there must be valid reasons for the allocation being reduced at the RE
stage. The Committee finds that whereas the expenditure figures under the Domestic Budgetary Support (DBS)
exceeded the funds allocated during the Ninth Plan, position was very different with regard to funds allocated under
Externally Aided Projects (EAP). Against provision of Rs. 4630.75 crores under EAP, expenditure was only Rs.
3118.91 crores, indicating a shortfall of Rs. 1511.84 crores.  
3.2       The Committee notes that the approved outlay for the Tenth Plan stands at Rs. 26,126 crores which is almost
double the Ninth Plan allocation. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that position has remained virtually
the same in the first three years of the Tenth Plan as evident during the Ninth Plan. Allocated funds continued to be
reduced at the RE stage and even those reduced funds remained under utilized:-

3.3       The Committee is not hopeful about full utilization of allocated funds in 2004-05. The Committee expresses its
serious concern over the element of unspent balances available under majority of the schemes during the first three
years of the Tenth Plan. The very fact that unspent balances continue to be available from year to year under any
scheme can lead to only two conclusions. Either the projected allocation has not been based on a scientific assessment
or failure of the implementing agencies in reaching the targeted beneficiaries. Both the situations need serious
review/rethinking of implementation process of such schemes. The Committee would, accordingly, impress upon the
Department to take remedial measures in the matter.
IV        NATIONAL RURAL HEALTH MISSION  
4.1       The Committee has been informed that National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) (2005-12) is to be launched
throughout the country in April, 2005 with special emphasis on eighteen  states with weak health infrastructure
including eight EAG States (U.P, M.P, Bihar, Rajasthan, Orissa, Jharkhand, Uttaranchal and Chattisgarh), eight NE
States, Himachal Pradesh, and Jammu & Kashmir. The Mission aims to provide comprehensive integrated primary
healthcare services, including RCH services and National Disease Control Programmes.
4.2       The Committee notes that under NRHM, the gaps in the existing scenario of rural health care are to be addressed
by creation of a cadre of community level functionaries called Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) to assist the
Angandwadi Worker and ANM at village level. The general norm for selection will be one ASHA per 1000 population
to be selected by the community and the process of selection would involve meeting of Gram Sabha and Gram
Panchayat. Following are some of the other anticipated Mission outcomes:-
Ø
      Raising CHCs to the level of Indian Public Health standard
Ø      Increasing utilization of First Referral units from less than 20% (2002) to more than 75% by 2010.
4.3       The Committee notes that NRHM is the most ambitious Project proposed to be launched in the Health and
Family Welfare Sector. Mission has received the Cabinet approval very recently, i.e. 4 th January, 2005. States are being
now advised to undertake preparatory activities. The Committee has been given to understand that in view of the recent
Cabinet approval, requirement for activities under NRHM could not be included in the proposal sent to the Planning
Commission. A minimum of Rs. 600 crores will be required as additional budgetary support during 2005-06.          
4.4       Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are very much required in the present scenario. The Committee
observes that divergent activities not only of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, but also number of other
Ministries are proposed to be implemented in an integrated manner. Two Departments of the Ministry-Health and
Family Welfare have been integrated for optimum utilization of financial resource and manpower. The Committee,
however, has a word of caution in this regard. Both the Departments as separate entities were already implementing 
large number of schemes and supervising institutions falling under their respective jurisdiction. Not only this, quite a
few programmes under both the Departments were not being administered effectively due to a very weak monitoring
mechanism relying only on state figures. The Committee feels that with the convergence of a number of Health and
Family Welfare  Schemes under NRHM, effective monitoring may not be feasible.  The Committee would, therefore,

emphasise that dilution of services at present available separately under the two Departments must be avoided at all
costs.       
V         RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES          
5.1
              Rural Family Welfare Services are meant to provide comprehensive primary health care to the masses at grass-
root level. The primary health care infrastructure has been developed as a three tier system and is based on the following
population norms:-
Center Plain area Hilly/Tribal/Difficult area
Sub-Center 5000 3000
Primary Health Center 30,000 20,000
Community Health Center 1,20,000 80,000
 
5.2       The Sub-Center is the lowest level of the primary health care system which is manned by one Auxiliary Nurse
Mid-wife (ANM) and one Male Health Worker (Multi Purpose Worker-MPW). In addition, one LHV is entrusted with
the supervision of 6 sub-centres.
5.3       Govt. of India bears the salary of ANMs as per state Govt. pay scales and honorarium for voluntary workers.
Rent @ Rs. 3000/- per annum and contingency @ Rs  3200/- per annum is also borne by the Central Govt. Salary of
male worker is provided by the State Govt.
5.4       Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Community Health Centers (CHCs) are established and managed by the
State Govts. under the Minimum Needs Programme/ Basis Minimum Service Programme. PHC acts as referral unit for
six Sub-Centers and CHC services as a referral center for four PHCs.
5.5
                   The Budgetary allocation of Rs. 1532.71 crores in BE 2004-05 was increased to Rs. 1722.10 crores at RE
level and it has further been increased to Rs. 1869.20 crores in BE 2005-06. The Department has submitted that the
enhanced allocation in BE 2005-06 will be utilized in funding the additional sub-centers whose number has increased
from existing 1,37,311 to 1,42,655 and also to meet the increased unit cost due to enhanced DA and other miscellaneous
expenditures. There is marginal saving of Rs. 4.50 crores in 2004-05 which is due to unspent balance lying with
States/UTs and less infrastructure in NE states.
5.6       Additional Sub-Centres required as per 1991 Census are 8669 and as per 2001 population are 26,478. Against a
Tenth Plan target of opening of 8181 Sub-centres fixed by the Planning Commission, annual target for 2003-04 and
2004-05 is 1941 in each year. The Committee has been given to understand that after Cabinet approval in January,2004,
funds for establishing new Sub-Centres @ Rs. 10,000 each were released on February 2004. The Committee, however,
notes that as per the figures made available to it, 5344 Sub-Centres are supposed to be established in 2003-04 and 2004-
05. Three states are the major beneficiaries, with 1954 Sub-Centres established in Andhra Pradesh, 706 Sub-Centres in
Madhya Pradesh and 2230 Sub-Centres in U. P. The Committee has been given to understand that the target in
establishment of Sub-Centres is given by the Planning Commission for respective States/UTs. The Committee would
like to be apprised of exact number of Sub-Centres established (state-wise) during the first three years of Tenth
Plan.
5.7       As per 2001 population, 4977 more PHCs are needed to be established in the country. The Committee notes that
only  234 PHCs were established during 2003-04 and 2004-05, 104 were established in Andhra Pradesh and 136 PHCs
in Himachal Pradesh. The capital cost of one PHC is Rs. 24.50 lakhs with a recurring liability of Rs. 13 lakhs. This
expenditure is met by the State Govt. under the PMGY programme.

5.8       The Committee is surprised to note that some states have already established PHCs in excess of the prescribed
norms.   There are also states where shortfall in the number of PHCs is evident. Against a population norm of 30,000 per
PHC, average rural population (2001) per PHC is 45,095 in Bihar, 37,169 in Madhya Pradesh, 36348 in Tripura 36,169
in U.P. 49,231 in West Bengal and 1,18,090 in Delhi. The Committee is not convinced by the clarifications of the
Department that the target for establishment of PHCs is given by the Planning Commission to the respective States/UTs
and it is the responsibility of the State/UTs to establish them. The Committee strongly feels that with funds being
provided under PMGY scheme, it is the responsibility of the Department to monitor the establishment of PHCs .
5.9       The Committee finds that the same problem is there with regard to CHCs also. Arunachal Pradesh, U.P,
Mizoram, Maharashtra, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep and Pondicherry have excess infrastructure in terms
of CHCs .Capital cost of one CHCs is Rs. 80.50 lakhs with a recurring liability of Rs. 27.00 lakhs is met by the State
Govts. under the PMGY programme. The Committee is of the opinion  that in view of the non-adherence to  the
prescribed population norms, whether short or excess by majority of the states, it is time that a review of the existing
population norms are looked into by the Department.    
5.10     The Committee’s attention has been drawn by an evaluation study of 1040 Sub-Centres covering 300 districts of
14 major states conducted by   National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER). The findings of the
evaluation were submitted on 22
nd November, 2004. Major recommendations/conclusions of NCAER included in its
Report submitted on 22.11.04 are as under:-
(i)                  Lack of permanent Sub-Centres building is an important constraint in the functioning of Sub-Centres. 
Sub-Centres in rented buildings keep on shifting, thus creating information gap among the users.
Permanent SC buildings provide an incentive to furnish it properly. Permanently owned building is a pre-
condition for improving the quality of delivery and utilization of services. It is also desirable that ANM
and Anganwadi Workers both have accommodation in a common compound to avoid duplication of
certain services. For better service delivery, SC building should be located at a central place.
 
(ii)
                Shortage of staff is quite high and almost half the SCs are functioning without Male Health Worker. The
data shows that significantly higher proportion of respondents from the SCs with both ANM and MHW
are “fully satisfied”, therefore appointing MHW alongwith ANM in all the SCs should be done on
priority basis.
 
(iii)       Irregularity in the disbursement of salary to the staff is a serious problem especially in Jharkhand, Bihar,
Orrisa and Utter Pradesh.
 
5.11     The Committee understands that the Report of the NCAER study is at present under the considerations of the
Department. The Committee would like to emphasise that the Department should initiate action at the earliest for
strengthening the functioning of Sub-Centres, PHCs and CHCs, the only service providers to the targeted beneficiaries
in the remote and inaccessible  areas in the country. A beginning can be made with the fourteen states where the sample
study was conducted by NCAER. The Committee would also like to emphasise that a similar study is also required to be
undertaken with regard to functionaries of both PHCs and CHCs which are also the main service providers likes Sub-
Centres. 
5.12     The Committee would like to point out that demographically weak states have higher birth rate and Infant
Mortality Rate. The workload of ANMs in these states is thus higher. The Committee, therefore, feels that in such states,
sanctioning of ANMs should be based on existing norms as per 2001 population. At the same time, the Department
should also closely monitor the filling up of all the sanctioned posts of ANMs.

VI        URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES 
6.1       A total of 1083 Urban Family welfare centres of three types and 871 health posts of four types depending upon
the staff sanctioned and population covered are functioning in different states.  Out reach Family welfare and primary
health care services in urban areas with emphasis in urban slum areas are provided through these centres.
6.2       The Committee observes that a very limited number of Urban Family Welfare Centres and Urban Health Posts
i.e. 1083 centres and 871 health posts have been sanctioned so far. These limited Centres/Health Posts are also not
evenly spread across the country. Out of the total Centres and Health Posts, major beneficiary states are :-

            Rs. 65.04 crore and Rs. 58.00 crores have been provided under those schemes under Center/Post respectively.
 
6.3       The Committee has noted that the plan allocation under ‘Urban Family Welfare Services’ was Rs. 121.00 crores
during 2004-05 which has been increased to Rs. 133.00 crores in BE 2005-06. The increased allocation will be utilized
to meet the likely increase in pay and allowances of staff.
6.4       The Committee has been informed that the task of evaluating Urban Family Welfare Centers and Urban Health
Posts has been entrusted to Inter- national Institute of Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai in April, 2004.  Although
Interim Reports of the evaluation study have been received in January, 2005, final report is still awaited.
6.5       The Committee has taken seriously the under-utilization of funds under Urban Family Welfare Services for a
number of years in succession and the reason being the same. The Department perhaps did not take any remedial steps
to improve the situation. The Committee feels that based on the recommendations of the evaluation study, steps will be
taken for strengthening/expansion of the scheme.   
 
VII      REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME (RCH)
 
7.1       RCH is the flagship programme of the Govt. on Reproductive Child and Maternal Health. A paradigm shift is
envisaged in the manner in which the RCH Programme has been conceptualized and implemented based upon key
learning from the first phase of the Programme (1997-2002).   RCH-II is set to start from April, 2005.
7.2       The Committee observes that RCH-II programme is envisaged as umbrella programme which will integrate all
the related and interlinked stand alone schemes into a single composite programme. All the schemes under the Flexible
Pool will cease to be prescriptive and will only provide generic guidelines. The key characteristic of the Flexible Pool is
to enable the states to devise need-based intervention and undertake decentralized planning. The Flexible Pool will be
operated by providing the State with a financial envelope based upon which each state will formulate its own PIP rather
than subscriber to multiple schemes.
            Accordingly the budget heads of the Department are also proposed to be rationalized and compressed into four
omnibus schemes:-
Ø
      Operational support to the states -  committed expenditure such as salary of ANMs, grants to State Training
Institutes, free distribution of contraceptives

Ø      Operational cost of Institution supported by the Department -grants to central institutions like NIHFW,ICMR
etc.
Ø      Activities centrally implemented by the Department - procurement of drugs and equipment, vaccines for routine
immunization etc.
Ø      Activities in the State Programme Implementation Plan (PIP) –base flexible pool to support state PIPs.    
7.3     The Committee has also been informed that all the externally aided projects are proposed to be merged with
RCH-II. All the Development partners   supporting the Department have agreed in principle to move towards a sector-
wise approach. However, a transition period has been sought by them to allow them time to complete their existing
commitments and to re-align that current programme with the paradigm shift. Another important initiative is to have a
common programme. Management structure and monitoring evaluations arrangement for RCH programme at state and
district levels by April, 2005. The Committee would however like to emphasize that besides organizing workshops
meeting with state/district level officials, inspections both regular/surprise by designated central officials should also be
initiated   The Committee welcomes all these very significant initiatives being taken by the Department and hopes that
they would be implemented as envisaged to get the desired results.     
7.4       Total Allocation for RCH Programme during the Tenth Plan is Rs. 2676 crores. The Committee notes that there
is a significant enhancement in the allocation of funds for this programme during the first three years of the Tenth Plan.
However, utilization of allocated funds has failed to meet the steady increase in the allocation of funds. Funds allocated
in the beginning of the year had to be invariably reduced at the RE stage and even these  allocated funds remained
under-utilized.
            Instead of there being any improvement, situation has worsened during 2004-05 BE  2004-05 provision of Rs.
710.51 crores had to be reduced to Rs. 485.93 crores. Actual expenditure during 2004-05 (9
th March, 05) is only Rs.
306.32 crores. Factors responsible for this dismal performance level are limited availability of Donor funding, lower
than anticipated demand for funds, non-submission of utilization certificates and availability of unspent balances with
the states.
7.5       The Committee observes that more or less the same factors were responsible for under-utilisation in the first two
years of the Tenth Plan.   The Committee notes that an enhanced allocation of Rs. 1380.68 crores has been made for
2005-06, based upon an assessment of demands of the States/UTs, and the committed liabilities of the States. The
Committee views with serious concern the availability of unspent funds with different states under this programme.
7.6       In its Second Report presented to the Parliament on 26
th August,2004, the Committee had expressed its serious
concern over the availability of unspent balances amounting to Rs. 912.80 crores with different states against a total
allocation of Rs. 2217.00 crores under RCH Programme since its inception in 1997-98. In response thereto, the
Department in its Action Taken Note have informed that unspent balances stand reduced to Rs. 809.26 crores from Rs.
912.80 crores whereas the actual unspent balances were even less. The Committee is not inclined to accept this feedback
for the simple reason that as per the latest information given by the Department itself, against a total allocation of Rs.
2461.57 crores, utilization figures are Rs. 1638.49 crores and unspent balances are Rs. 823.07 crores. This clearly
indicates that funds are being released under the RCH Programme on regular basis, availability of unspent balances with
states making no difference. Position with regard to a few States found  alarming last year by the Committee, continues

   7.7          The Committee has been informed that a series of meetings/workshops on the issue of unspent balances were
held at Kolkata, Trivandrum, Daman and Guwahati during September to Novemeber,2004 by the Department with
different States Govts. The purpose behind it was to assess the volume of unspent balances, to assist the State Govt
Authorities in preparation of utilization certificates and to point out the  inconsistencies between the audit report and the
utilization certificates. Some major constraints emerged were:-
(i)
                  Lack of monitoring capacity of the programmes/ interventions by the district and block.
(ii)                Weakness in managerial capacity at the state/district level.
(iii)               Less interaction between the officials of the Central Govt. and those at state and district level.
(iv)              Weak financial management specially at district and block level.
The Committee notes that the Department has initiated some remedial measures, creating State and District
Management Units engaging qualified Managers, Accounts persons and a qualified Financial Expert which are the 
required initiatives. The proposal of the Govt. to continue with the process of organizing workshops and meetings with
state and district level officers is welcome.   The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that besides organizing
workshops/meetings with State/district level officials, inspections both regular/surprise  by designated Central Govt.
officials should also be initiated.
7.8     The Committee has some apprehensions about the feasibility of the new methodology proposed to be adopted for
release of central financial assistance under RCH-II. In view of very poor performance of the various State Govts. in
majority of the components of RCH programme so far, the flexibility now proposed to be given to them may prove to be
counter-productive. The Committee is of the view that the Department in the initial years will have to play a pro-active

a very discouraging position. Against an allocation of Rs. 109.88 crores under ANM scheme, only 6335 ANMs were
given contractual appointment. Similarly, for PHN/Staff Nurse,  against an allocation of Rs. 31.04 crores, only 1467
PHNs could be given contractual appointment. Allocation for Lab Technicians stands at Rs. 8.37 crores, number of
contractual Lab Technician is only 381.  Similarly, for hiring of SM Consultant against an allocation of Rs. 3.61 crore,
only 1054 Consultants  could be appointed. For hiring of private Anaesthetists, Rs. 83.73 lakhs have been provided and
number of Anaesthetists hired is only  1059. In a number of interventions, although funds have been duly released not
even a single contractual appointment seems to have been made in the States of Bihar, Jharkhand, Tripura, Uttaranchal,
Karnataka. In the case of other states also, level of physical achievement is very poor when compared with the quantum
of funds released.
 7.12    Non-availability of sufficiently qualified manpower in the states is the main reason cited for non-achievement of
contractual appointments of ANMs/PHNs/SNs/ Lab Technicians. Sufficient number of Anaesthetists in the private
sector is not available at sub-district level.   Honorarium of Rs. 800/- per  visit was not found adequate enough to

of the ground realities. Not only this, practice of funds being released without showing any achievement needs a review

VIII     JANANI SURAKSHA YOJNA (NATIONAL MATERNITY BENEFIT SCHEME)
 
8.1       The Committee has been informed that the National Maternity Benefit Scheme is being revised as Janani
Suraksha Yojna (JSY) with the aim of promotion of institutional delivery to bring down the high Maternal Mortality
Rate. Under this scheme, a BPL mother will get Rs. 1000 per girl child and Rs. 400/- per male child, if delivered in a
health institution as against uniform rate of Rs. 500/- per child for the first two live births under the earlier scheme.
Besides, transport assistance upto Rs. 150/- and incentive to Dais @ Rs. 200/150 for female/male child has been
envisaged in lieu of appropriate antenatal and postnatal care and referral for institutional delivery. The scheme is also
aimed to operationalise FRUs at district levels to ensure 24 hrs services for improved delivery.
8.2       The Committee observes that exercise of revision of this scheme has been going on for the last  two-years.   As a
result, funds allocated have remained under-utilized. Against the allocation of Rs. 500 crores in the Tenth Plan, the
expenditure for first two years is only Rs. 87.57 crores and the balance available for the remaining period is Rs. 300.43
crores. The Committee feels that there should be no further delay and finalization of the schemes should be expedited. 
The Committee would also like to emphasize that the Department should not be complacent by just revising the scheme,
rather an effective monitoring mechanism should be evolved for its proper implementation.
8.3       The Committee has observed that under the existing scheme, there is no mechanism to ascertain the exact
number of actual beneficiaries of the scheme. The Department has been estimating the number of beneficiaries on the
basis of amount of grants released to the District Authorities. The Committee feels that under the proposed revised
scheme, there should be an inbuilt mechanism so that there is periodic survey to verify the exact number of
beneficiaries. The Committee also observes that state wise details of estimated number of beneficiaries indicate that
those states where need for population stabilization measures is the most do not seem to be taking benefit of this
scheme. The Committee is of the opinion that the revised scheme should be given due publicity, specially in
backward/tribal areas.
8.4       The Committee has also noticed that under the existing Scheme due to unspent balances, non-receipt/ late receipt
of UCs/Audited accounts/receipt of incomplete/incorrect documents, there was improper and under utilization of
allocated funds. This was evident in respect of all the States in the country. The Committee, would therefore, like to
emphasize that all preventive measures need to be taken to avoid such problems/shortcomings under the revised
scheme.

XII      ACCEPTANCE OF FAMILY PLANNING METHODS
12.1     The Committee is concerned to note that the acceptance of vasectomy in comparison to tubectomy has been low
for many years. Major reason as cited for low acceptance of vasectomy are: -
(i)
                  Lack of correct information on vasectomy among men resulting in wrong beliefs, myths and fear.
(ii)                Attitude of men towards family planning.
(iii)               Limited availability of trained manpower in ‘No Scalpel Vasectomy (NSV) which has been recently
introduced as simple, safer and easier male sterilization technique.
 
12.2     The Committee notes that a number of remedial majors like media and visual publicity, Training of doctors and
NSV and involvement of IMA in increasing awareness among private doctors in this regard, have been initiated by the
Department during 2004-05.  The Committee also observes that on the basis of inputs received from EAG states, the
compensation package for undergoing Tubectomy, Vasectomy and IUD insertion has been revised from 2003-04.  The
Committee hopes that with these measures there would be an increase in the acceptance level of male acceptance of
family planning methods. 
XIII   ACTIVITIES IN NORTH-EAST REGION
13.1     The Committee has been informed that the target population in the NE Region for provision of FW services such
as pregnant women, infants & children, and eligible couples constitute only 3.5% of the total population of the country. 
Besides, the number of Sub-Centes in the NE Region is also 5.5% of the total Sub-Centres of the Country.  Thus, the
potential of the Department of Family Welfare to spend the 10% of its total allocation is limited and the targeted
expenditure under FW programme in the NE Region cannot be met.  This is possible only if new infrastructure is
established in the Region or some new schemes, specifically for NE Region, are formulated and taken up for
implementation, which would require initiation of new schemes and thus require in-principle approval of the Planning
Commission. The Committee is not in agreement to the suggestion of the Department for being exempted from
earmarking the mandatory allocation of 10% for the NE region.  The Committee feels that the appropriate action would
be to initiate new schemes including those aimed at establishing new Primary Health Care Institutions and also
adequately augmenting staff strength in NE Region. 
13.2     The Committee has been given to understand that with the launching of National Rural Health Mission, a
steering Committee has been set up in the Department which will also be responsible for implementation of Family
Welfare programmes in the NE Region. An officer in the Department has been specifically deputed for this purpose.
The Committee was also informed that budget provision for NE states for 2005-06 has been enhanced by 30%. The
Secretary assured the Committee that with these initiatives, there would be proper focus on this remote and inaccessible

540 per 100,000 live births. The fact remains that there are some problem areas in data collection. Non-availability of
reliable estimates of maternal mortality has been admitted by the Department also in its Annual Report (2004-05).   The
Committee notes that an expert group has been constituted in the Department which is looking into the modalities of
carrying out a survey for collection of data on Maternal Mortality.  A Pilot survey for this has already been completed.
Similar problems may be there in respect of other health indicators also. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that
the Department should carry out a comparative analysis of findings of NFHS-I and NFHS-II in order to understand the
factors responsible for discrepancies in the two Survey Reports. The Committee would also like to emphasise that the
entire Family Welfare planning is based on the National Surveys being conducted at regular intervals. Therefore, it
should be ensured that accurate data is made the basis of all health surveys. This can be achieved to a large extent by
monitoring of data being obtained specially from the states not performing well by involving Central teams also in the
collection of data, to the extent possible. (Para 1.5)
 
II         TENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN-MID TERM APPRAISAL
2.5       The Committee is constrained to observe that the expected levels of some of the indicators by the terminal year
of the Tenth Plan are very high when compared with the actual achievement level reached by the end of Ninth Plan, i.e
2002.   The Committee feels that the percentage of performance reached at the end of the Ninth Plan was virtually the
same in respect of these indicators. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the immediate goal of the
Department/State Govt./implementing agencies should be put to a sustained exercise in motion where under the weakest
performing districts (state-wise) are identified and targeted interventions are initiated, accompanied by regular
monitoring.  (Para 2.5)  
 
III        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
3.2       The Committee notes that the approved outlay for the Tenth Plan stands at Rs. 26,126 crores which is almost
double the Ninth Plan allocation. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that position has remained virtually
the same in the first three years of the Tenth Plan as evident during the Ninth Plan. Allocated funds continued to be
reduced at the RE stage and even those reduced funds remained under

IV        NATIONAL RURAL HEALTH MISSION  
            The Committee notes that NRHM is the most ambitious Project proposed to be launched in the Health and
Family Welfare Sector. Mission has received the Cabinet approval very recently, i.e. 4
th January, 2005. States are being
now advised to undertake preparatory activities. The Committee has been given to understand that in view of the recent
Cabinet approval, requirement for activities under NRHM could not be included in the proposal sent to the Planning
Commission. A minimum of Rs. 600 crores will be required as additional budgetary support during 2005-06.

4.4       Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are very much required in the present scenario. The Committee
observes that divergent activities not only of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, but also number of other
Ministries are proposed to be implemented in an integrated manner. Two Departments of the Ministry-Health and
Family Welfare have been integrated for optimum utilization of financial resource and manpower. The Committee,
however, has a word of caution in this regard. Both the Departments as separate entities were already implementing 
large number of schemes and supervising institutions falling under their respective jurisdiction. Not only this, quite a
few programmes under both the Departments were not being administered effectively due to a very weak monitoring
mechanism relying only on state figures. The Committee feels that with the convergence of a number of Health and
Family Welfare  Schemes under NRHM, effective monitoring may not be feasible.  The Committee would, therefore,
emphasise that dilution of services at present available separately under the two Departments must be avoided at all
costs.    (Para 4.4)   
           
V         RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES          
 The Committee would like to be apprised of exact number of Sub-Centres established (state-wise) during the
first three years of Tenth Plan. (Para 5.6)
            The Committee is surprised to note that some states have already established PHCs in excess of the prescribed
norms.   There are also states where shortfall in the number of PHCs is evident. Against a population norm of 30,000 per
PHC, average rural population (2001) per PHC is 45,095 in Bihar, 37,169 in Madhya Pradesh, 36348 in Tripura 36,169
in U.P. 49,231 in West Bengal and 1,18,090 in Delhi. The Committee is not convinced by the clarifications of the
Department that the target for establishment of PHCs is given by the Planning Commission to the respective States/UTs
and it is the responsibility of the State/UTs to establish them. The Committee strongly feels that with funds being
provided under PMGY scheme, it is the responsibility of the Department to monitor the establishment of PHCs. (Para
5.8)
The Committee is of the opinion that in view of the non-adherence to the prescribed population norms, whether
short or excess by majority of the states, it is time that a review of the existing population norms are looked into by the
Department.  (Para 5.9)
            The Committee understands that the Report of the NCAER study is at present under the considerations of the
Department. The Committee would like to emphasise that the Department should initiate action at the earliest for
strengthening the functioning of Sub-Centres, PHCs and CHCs, the only service providers to the targeted beneficiaries
in the remote and inaccessible areas in the country. A beginning can be made with the fourteen states where the sample
study was conducted by NCAER. The Committee would also like to emphasise that a similar study is also required to be
undertaken with regard to functionaries of both PHCs and CHCs which are also the main service providers likes Sub-
Centres. 
5.12     The Committee would like to point out that demographically weak states have higher birth rate and Infant
Mortality Rate. The workload of ANMs in these states is thus higher. The Committee, therefore, feels that in such states,
sanctioning of ANMs should be based on existing norms as per 2001 population. At the same time, the Department
should also closely monitor the filling up of all the sanctioned posts of ANMs.   (Para 5.11)
 
VI        URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES 
            The Committee has taken seriously the under-utilization of funds under Urban Family Welfare Services for a
number of years in succession and the reason being the same. The Department perhaps did not take any remedial steps

to improve the situation. The Committee feels that based on the recommendations of the evaluation study, steps will be

VII      REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME (RCH)
 
                     The Committee would however like to emphasize that besides organizing workshops meeting with
state/district level officials, inspections both regular/surprise by designated central officials should also be initiated   The
Committee welcomes all these very significant initiatives being taken by the Department and hopes that they would be
implemented as envisaged to get the desired results.  (Para 7.3)   
 
            The Committee observes that more or less the same factors were responsible for under-utilisation in the first two
years of the Tenth Plan.   The Committee notes that an enhanced allocation of Rs. 1380.68 crores has been made for

Committee views with serious concern the availability of unspent funds with different states under this programme.
(Para 7.5)

The Committee notes that the Department has initiated some remedial measures, creating State and District
Management Units engaging qualified Managers, Accounts persons and a qualified Financial Expert which are the
required initiatives. The proposal of the Govt. to continue with the process of organizing workshops and meetings with
state and district level officers is welcome.   The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that besides organizing
workshops/meetings with State/district level officials, inspections both regular/surprise by designated Central Govt.
officials should also be initiated.    (Para 7.7)
 
The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the Department should evolve a system whereunder besides State
Govts. other Stakeholders also have a decisive role to play.  (Para 7.8)  
A comparative analysis of funds released and  achievement level of physical targets of these interventions present a
very discouraging position. Against an allocation of Rs. 109.88 crores under ANM scheme, only 6335 ANMs were
given contractual appointment. Similarly, for PHN/Staff Nurse,  against an allocation of Rs. 31.04 crores, only 1467
PHNs could be given contractual appointment. Allocation for Lab Technicians stands at Rs. 8.37 crores, number of
contractual Lab Technician is only 381.  Similarly, for hiring of SM Consultant against an allocation of Rs. 3.61 crore,
only 1054 Consultants  could be appointed. For hiring of private Anaesthetists, Rs. 83.73 lakhs have been provided and
number of Anaesthetists hired is only  1059. In a number of interventions, although funds have been duly released not
even a single contractual appointment seems to have been made in the States of Bihar, Jharkhand, Tripura, Uttaranchal,
Karnataka. In the case of other states also, level of physical achievement is very poor when compared with the quantum
of funds released. (Para 7.11)
            Non-availability of sufficiently qualified manpower in the states is the main reason cited for non-achievement of
contractual appointments of ANMs/PHNs/SNs/ Lab Technicians. Sufficient number of Anaesthetists in the private
sector is not available at sub-district level.   Honorarium of Rs. 800/- per  visit was not found adequate enough to
motivate Safe Motherhood Consultants being mainly lady doctors to travel to remote areas. The Committee feels that all
these interventions which would continue to be available under the flexible RCH pool will have to be revamped in view
of the ground realities. Not only this, practice of funds being released without showing any achievement needs a review
in view of non-utilization of such Govt. funds for considerable period.  (Para7.12)
 
             RCH camps were initially permitted for 117 districts of 21 states and 7 UTs and then to all the districts of EAG
states, i.e. Bihar,Orissa, M.P, Rajasthan, Uttaranchal, U.P, Jharkhand and Chattisgarh Rs. 19.70 crores has been released
so far and total number of camps organised is 7283. The Committee has been given to understand that funds are released
to the states as per their proposal and also subject to the submission of UCs and Audit Report for the earlier years. The
Committee notes that a variety of services are being provided in the RCH camps by the states. As per the information
made available to the Committee, states like Assam, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, J&K, M.P, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, 
Uttaranchal, and U.P have been very active in holding RCH camps. However, the Committee is constrained to observe
that in the case of EAG states like Bihar, Chattisgarh, Jharkhand and Orissa no information is available inspite of there
being provision to hold RCH camps in all the districts of EAG states. The Committee strongly feels that these states
should be persuaded to take maximum benefit of this facility.    (Para7.14)        
 
VIII     JANANI SURAKSHA YOJNA (NATIONAL MATERNITY BENEFIT SCHEME)
 
The Committee observes that exercise of revision of this scheme has been going on for the last  two-years.   As a
result, funds allocated have remained under-utilized. Against the allocation of Rs. 500 crores in the Tenth Plan, the
expenditure for first two years is only Rs. 87.57 crores and the balance available for the remaining period is Rs. 300.43
crores. The Committee feels that there should be no further delay and finalization of the schemes should be expedited. 
The Committee would also like to emphasize that the Department should not be complacent by just revising the scheme,
rather an effective monitoring mechanism should be evolved for its proper implementation. (Para 8.2)
            The Committee has observed that under the existing scheme, there is no mechanism to ascertain the exact

number of actual beneficiaries of the scheme. The Department has been estimating the number of beneficiaries on the
basis of amount of grants released to the District Authorities. The Committee feels that under the proposed revised
scheme, there should be an inbuilt mechanism so that there is periodic survey to verify the exact number of
beneficiaries. The Committee also observes that state wise details of estimated number of beneficiaries indicate that
those states where need for population stabilization measures is the most do not seem to be taking benefit of this
scheme. The Committee is of the opinion that the revised scheme should be given due publicity, specially in
backward/tribal areas. (Para 8.3)
 
            The Committee has also noticed that under the existing Scheme due to unspent balances, non-receipt/ late receipt
of UCs/Audited accounts/receipt of incomplete/incorrect documents, there was improper and under utilization of
allocated funds. This was evident in respect of all the States in the country. The Committee, would therefore, like to
emphasize that all preventive measures need to be taken to avoid such problems/shortcomings under the revised
scheme.  (Para 8.4)  
 
IX        STRENGTHENING OF IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME & ERADICATION OF POLIO     
 
The Committee is not inclined to agree with the justification for underutilization of funds  given by the
Department.  The Committee feels that the Department will have to focus on State- specific strategies for optimum and
judicious utilisation of allocated funds.  The Committee observes that as per RHS-2002, immunization level of children
is 49%.  The Department will have to make concerted efforts to reach the target of 100% coverage of children under
immunization against six preventable diseases by the end of Tenth Plan, 2007.   (Para 9.4)
 
9.6       The Committee is a bit apprehensive of the commitment of the Government to eradicate all strains of the
poliovirus in near future. The Department has now confirmed that as on 14
th March 2005, 136 cases of Polio were
reported in the country in 2004, out of which 82 were from U.P and that too, 21 from Moradabad and 12 from Badaun
district. Analysis of cases in Moradabad and Baduan has shown that poor micro-planning, training and social
mobilization are the main factors responsible for high rate of Polio in these districts. (Para 9.6)
 
The Committee finds that the justification given by the Department that due to the poor quality of rounds
undertaken between July to Sept.2004 because of floods can not be considered very convincing.   The Committee feels
that the Department has to anticipate this kind of situations and take remedial action well in time. The Committee hopes
that with the high quality of supplementary immunization activity planed for 2005, things would improve in the State. 
The Committee would also like to emphasize that the remedial measures as initiated in affected districts of UP in the
wake of increase in the number of Polio cases may also be undertaken in all the affected districts of Bihar.  (Para 9.8)
 
X     JANSANKHYA STHIRTHA KOSH
           
            The Committee expresses its serious concerns about the fate of a project initiated with laudable objective.  It
took three years to implement the decision of setting of the Kosh. Almost two years have passed since then and the seed
money of Rs. 100 crores available under the Kosh is lying unutilized. The Committee can understand the total lack of
contributions/donations from any sector. The Committee, however, fails to understand the rationale for non-utilisation
of funds available under the Kosh.  The Committee finds that the approval of the Cabinet has been obtained for
reconstitution of the Kosh so as to increase its membership and establish it as an autonomous society, free to operate in
a non-bureaucratic mode.  The Committee would like to emphasize that adequate publicity about the availability of
funds under the Kosh for providing financial assistance for Projects on Population Stabilisation and also for inviting
contribution to the same needs to be given.  (Para 10.3)
 
XI        FREE DISTRIBUTION OF CONVENTIONAL CONTRACEPTIVE AND ITS SOCIAL MARKETING
 
The Committee is apprehensive of the justification as the reduction in allocation during 2004-05 is very marginal
for non-procurement of Laparoscopes whereas increase in the year 2005-06 is abnormally high for purchase of the same
item. The Committee therefore recommends that the allocation available for a specific purpose should be utilized in
proper, just and equitable manner. (Para 11.1)

11.5     The Committee observes that the initiative taken by the Hindustan latex Family Planning Promotion Trust in
selected districts of MP, Orissa, Jharkhand and Bihar is a positive development.    The Committee finds that another
area project on social marketing is being implemented by the Society for Women and Child Health   in four districts of
Haryana from April, 2000.  The Committee feels that the results of these two initiatives should be shared with other
reputed NGOs so as to motivate them to implement similar projects in other weak performing districts.  The Committee
is of the view that the Department may make an assessment in this regard and coordinate with the concerned State
Govts. and implementing agencies.  (Para 11.5)
 
XII      ACCEPTANCE OF FAMILY PLANNING METHODS
            The Committee notes that a number of remedial majors like media and visual publicity, Training of doctors and
NSV and involvement of IMA in increasing awareness among private doctors in this regard, have been initiated by the
Department during 2004-05.  The Committee also observes that on the basis of inputs received from EAG states, the
compensation package for undergoing Tubectomy, Vasectomy and IUD insertion has been revised from 2003-04.  The
Committee hopes that with these measures there would be an increase in the acceptance level of male acceptance of
family planning methods.  (Para 12.6)
 
XIII   ACTIVITIES IN NORTH-EAST REGION
The Committee is not in agreement to the suggestion of the Department for being exempted from earmarking the
mandatory allocation of 10% for the NE region.  The Committee feels that the appropriate action would be to initiate
new schemes including those aimed at establishing new Primary Health Care Institutions and also adequately
augmenting staff strength in NE Region.  (Para 13.1)
            The Committee has been given to understand that with the launching of National Rural Health Mission, a
steering Committee has been set up in the Department which will also be responsible for implementation of Family
Welfare programmes in the NE Region. An officer in the Department has been specifically deputed for this purpose.
The Committee was also informed that budget provision for NE states for 2005-06 has been enhanced by 30%. The
Secretary assured the Committee that with these initiatives, there would be proper focus on this remote and inaccessible
area. (Para 13.2)
            The Committee has, however, a word of caution for the Department. Committee’s attention has been drawn by
media reports about diversion of Central Funds meant for NE states due to pressure of underground outfits. The
Committee understands that this issue was discussed in a recent meeting chaired by the Cabinet secretary. The
Committee would like to emphasise that in States like Manipur, Nagalnd and some parts of Assam, due to underground
activities, impact of various Central Family Welfare Programmes is not visible. Infrastructure is simply not there. There
is acute shortage of doctors and other allied staff. The Committee is of the view that proper monitoring mechanism is
evolved so that the enhances funds meant for Family Welfare services in N.E. region are appropriately utilized and
relevant infrastructure is established. Inspection by Central teams, both regular and surprise, may also be conducted,
specially in view of reported diversion of Central funds. (Para 13.3)

XV       ANNUAL REVIEW REPORTS OF THE DEPARTMENT FOR 2003-04
 
The Committee views with serious concern the irregularities in Annual Review Report 2003-04 of the
Department. The Committee strongly feels that irregular charging of states General side Expenditure to the Family

REPORT
The Food Safety and Standards (Amendment) Bill, 2014 (hereinafter referred to as the Bill)
was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 19 th February,2014 and referred to the Department related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare on the 24 th February, 2014 for
examination and report thereon.
2. As per the information furnished by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on the Bill,
the Parliament enacted the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act) to consolidate the laws
relating to food in the country, to lay down science-based standards for articles of food and to
regulate their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import. In pursuance to the same, the
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (Food Authority) was established in 2008. The Bill
seeks to amend sections 5 and 92 of the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006 (34 of 2006)
and to insert a new section, ‘section 7A’, to tide over the difficulties, affecting the overall
functioning and implementation of various provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, and
to delineate clearly the roles of the Chairperson, and the Chief Executive Officer of the authority
for its smooth functioning. It will also help in faster notification of standards of food products.
3. According to the Statement of Objects and Reasons (SOR), the Bill, proposes to: include
the Chief Executive Officer in the composition of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of
India; amend sub-section (1) of section 5 of FSS Act so as to provide that the provision regarding
one-third members being women, shall be applicable to the members referred to in clauses (b), (c),
(d), (f) and (g) of sub-section (1) of section 5 of the said Act; insert section 7A in the said Act
to address the need for continuity of policies, enabling the Chairperson to guide the affairs of the
Authority; amend Section 92 empowering the Authority to make regulations by notification with the
previous approval of the Central Government and after previous publication by empowering the
Central Government to dispense with the condition of previous publication in certain cases, in the
public interest.
4. However, the said Bill could not be taken up for examination due to preoccupation of the
Members of the previous Committee in the General Elections for the Sixteenth Lok Sabha and
subsequent dissolution of the Committee. After the reconstitution of the Committee, the Hon’ble
Chairman, Rajya Sabha had granted extension for a period of two months i.e. upto 31
st October,
2014 and another extension upto 5 th December, 2014 for examination and report on the Bill.
5. In the meeting of Committee held on 18 th September, 2014, the Secretary, Department of
Health and Family Welfare while giving presentation on the Bill informed that subsequent to
introduction of the Amendment Bill, the Lucknow Bench of Allahabad High Court in the W.P.(C)
No. 1717 (MB) of 2013 and the Supreme Court of India in Petition(C) No. 159/2012 directed the
Government to bring appropriate amendments in the Act to deal with the food adulteration sternly.
Accordingly, a note was being placed before the Cabinet for pursuing the Bill in its present form
or otherwise. Thereafter, Members raised issues of reported incidents of rampant adulteration in
food items highlighting the issues of unregulated sale of packaged water; adulterated milk and milk
products; contents of fertilizers/pesticides/insecticides in food grains/vegetables/fruits and impressed
upon the Department to take measures to check and curb such rampant food adulteration in the
food items in the country.
6. Subsequently, the Department vide its communication dated 25
th September, 2014 informed
that the Minister had approved the proposal for withdrawal of the Bill and it would be placed before
the Cabinet for consideration/approval. The Committee in its meeting held on 25 th September, 2014

2
considered the proposal of the Ministry and felt that no useful purpose would be served pursuing
the Bill if the Bill was to be withdrawn. The Committee, therefore, decided not to pursue the Bill
till a final decision is taken by the Cabinet as to whether the Government would pursue the Bill
or not.
7. The Department of Health and Family Welfare vide its communication dated 13
th November,
2014 submitted before the Committee as follows:
“the Cabinet in its meeting held on 05.11.2014 approved the proposal of the Department
of Health and Family Welfare for withdrawing the Food Safety and Standards (Amendment)
Bill, 2014 and a formal communication for withdrawal of the Bill will be sent in due
course of time.”
8. The Chairman of the Committee conveyed the contents of the communication to Members
of the Committee in its meeting held on 19
th November, 2014. In view of the Cabinet’s decision
for withdrawal of the Bill, the Committee decided not to pursue the Bill.
9. In view of the decision of the Cabinet to withdraw the Bill, the Committee observes
that no useful purpose will be served in examining the Bill. The Committee, has therefore,
decided not to pursue the Bill. The Committee also observes that immediate measures are
required to be taken to deal with incidents of rampant adulteration in food items in the
country and impresses upon the Government to give more teeth to the Food Safety and
Standards Act, 2006 and the Food Authority to tackle these incidents. The Committee
therefore recommends that Government may re-look into all aspects and bring a
comprehensive Bill at the earliest.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The Food Safety and Standards Act was enacted in the
year 2006 with a view to consolidate the laws relating to Food in
the country and to establish the Food Safety and Standards
Authority of India for laying down science-based standards for
articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage,
distribution, sale and import and to ensure availability of safe and
wholesome food for human consumption.
2. Sub-section (1) of section 5 of the said Act provides for
the composition of the Food Authority consisting of a Chairperson
and twenty-two members, which does not include the Chief
Executive Officer. It is proposed to include the Chief Executive
Officer in the composition of the Food Safety and Standards
Authority of India.
3. Further sub-section (1) of section 5 of the said Act
provides that one-third of the members shall be women in the
composition of the said Authority. Out of twenty-two Members of
the said Authority 12 members are nominated by the Central
Ministries, Departments, the States or Union territories. It is quite
difficult to ensure appointment of 1/3rd women members out of
these 12 members. This makes it imperative to appoint 7 women
members out of remaining 10 part-time members representing food
industry, consumers’ organisations, eminent food technologists and
scientists, farmers’ organisations and retailers’ organisations.
Therefore, it is proposed to amend sub-section (1) of section 5 of
the said Act so as to provide that the provision regarding one-third
members being women, shall be applicable to the members referred
to in clauses (b), (c), (d), (f) and (g) of sub-section (1) of section
5 of the said Act.
4. Section 5 of the said Act empowers the Central
Government to appoint the Chairperson in such a menner so as to
secure the highest standards of competence and relevant expertise.
The Chairperson is expected to not only guide the organisation in its
initial stages but also help in laying down systems, procedures and
structures to enable the said Authority to function as per the legal
mandate. The Act, however, does not specifically provide for this
essential role of guiding and overseeing the work of the said
Authority, though under section 16 of the Act, the said Authority is
mandated to regulate and monitor the manufacture, processing,
distribution, sale and import of food so as to ensure safe and
wholesome food. As laid down in the preamble to the Act, it is
necessary to provide a single line of command in the Food Authority
to provide direction and accountability. Therefore, it is proposed to
insert section 7A in the said Act to address the need for continuity

of policies, enabling the Chairperson to guide the affairs of the Food
Authority.
5. The section 92 empowers the said Authority to make
regulations by notification with the previous approval of the Central
Government and after previous publication. It is proposed to amend
the said section so as to empower the Central Government to
dispense with the condition of previous publication in certain cases,
in the public interest.

I. BACKGROUND
Observation/Recommendation
2.1 Several questions were asked and concerns expressed in the media and well meaning
quarters on the role of government agencies including Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
and Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) in approving and facilitating the trials, which was
against all laws of the land and even international ethical norms and rules; misuse of government
funds, man-power, facilities and infrastructure for a private project of dubious nature; use of logo
of National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), an official programme of the Union Government during
these vaccination drives to give it respectability and official endorsement; and above all the blatant
violation by PATH of all regulatory and ethical norms laid down by the Government of India for
the purpose as also possible violations of such norms prescribed and very scrupulously enforced
in the Country of its origin viz. United States of America. (Para 1.2)
Reply of the Ministry
2.2 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare constituted a Committee under the chairmanship
of Dr. S.S. Agarwal, former Director, Advanced Centre for Training, Research, Education on
Cancer to enquire into the alleged irregularities in the conduct of studies on Human Papilloma Virus
(HPV) vaccine by PATH in India. The Inquiry Committee in its report identified various deficiencies
in the planning and conduct of the study by PATH.
2.3 The Inquiry Committee was of the view that by whatever name it was called, the project
proposal had been carried out as research on human participants. As such, it had to follow all
guidelines and statutory requirements applicable on research on human participants. The Committee
further reported that the deaths were most probably unrelated to the vaccine under trial, as there was
no characteristic and uniform pattern of illness preceding the death, or temporal/spatial clustering. The
Committee also observed that in the absence of control group, it was not possible to say whether
there were excess deaths in the vaccinated group or not. Based on the data of background deaths
from routine mortality reporting system from the same area for the vaccination period as collected
by the Committee, it opined that overall death rate during the period of vaccination was not
significantly different, supporting the contention that reported deaths are independent of the HPV
vaccination. It further stated that internationally as on the 31
st January, 2010, 49 deaths were reported
in the USA against approximately 28 million doses of Gardasil vaccine distribution. Out of these, 28
deaths have been traced. According to CDC (Center for Disease Control, USA),there was no unusual
pattern or clustering to the deaths that would suggest that they were caused by the vaccine. It is
further added that these two vaccines are included in the National Immunization Programmes for
prevention of cervical cancer in women in many countries, like, USA, Canada, New Zealand, France
Germany, Sweden, Australia, Russia, UK, Mexico, etc.
2.4 The Inquiry Committee in its report had, however, identified various deficiencies in the
planning and conduct of the study by PATH. The gist of the same is as under:

4
● Consent forms and the actual implementation of the consent process.
● Method of monitoring the adverse effects and the serious adverse effects and
remedial measures for such events
● Inclusion of vulnerable tribal population groups.
● Blurring of distinction between National Immunization Program and PATH study.
● Insurance coverage for the study participants
● Free supply of vaccine by the manufacturer and the statement in the consent forms
that “you will not be charged for your daughter to receive the vaccine” that could
be considered as covert inducement and indirect coercion.
2.5 The penal provisions regarding the import of drugs are provided under Section 13 of the
Drugs and Cosmetics Act while penalty for manufacture, sale, etc., of drugs is provided under
Section27 of the Act. There are no specific penalties for violation of the provisions relating to
clinical trial under the Act.
2.6 The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 made under the said Act, under Part X-A of the
Rules have provisions for Import or Manufacture of New Drugs for Clinical trials or Marketing.
Under Rule 122 DA, the permissions to conduct clinical trials for new drugs/investigational new
drugs are granted by the Licensing Authority as defined in Rule 21(b) i.e. Drugs Controller General
(India). The Schedule Y to the said Rule provides detailed requirements for the Informed Consent
to be obtained from each study subject as well as responsibilities of the sponsor, investigator and
Ethics Committee. Rule122 DA empowers the DCG(I) to suspend cancel the permission issued to

II. NATURE OF PROJECT
Observation/Recommendation
2.14 Given the controversy surrounding the project, the Committee was keen to know from the
Government the exact nature of the project. The Committee noticed that there was fundamental
difference between the perceptions of Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) and Department
of Health Research (DHR)/Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on the actual nature of the
project. The DCGI was of the opinion that since human subjects, as part of the research, were
receiving invasive intervention like vaccines, the clinical trial rules must be enforced. Experts also
upheld these views and were very clear about it. However, PATH described the project as an
“observational study” “since it did not conform to the definition of clinical trial”. (Para 2.1)
2.15 The Committee found from the information furnished to it that ICMR representative on the
Project Advisory Committee not only opposed DCGI but also argued that the nature of the project
does not require them to follow the clinical trial rules, including reporting of serious adverse effects
within a specific time frame . (Para 2.2)
Reply of the Ministry
2.16 As per Schedule Y , Post Marketing Trials (Phase IV) are studies (other than routine
surveillance) performed after drug approval and related to the approved indication(s). These trials
go beyond the prior demonstration of the drug’s safety, efficacy and dose definition. These trials
may not be considered necessary at the time of new drug approval but may be required by the
Licensing Authority for optimizing the drug’s use. They may be of any type but should have valid
scientific objectives. Phase IV trials include additional drug-drug interaction(s), dose-response or
safety studies and trials designed to support use under the approved indication(s), e.g. mortality/
morbidity studies, epidemiological studies etc.
The objective of the PATH study was:
(i) To demonstrate suitable vaccine delivery strategy for HPV to 10-14 years old
adolescent girls.
(ii) To raise community awareness on HPV , cancer of the cervix and its prevention.
(iii) To gain experience in HPV vaccination and to build the evidence based of vaccine
delivery strategies for future introduction of HPV vaccines into Universal immunization
programs.
The primary outcome measures included:
1. Number and percent of eligible girls fully vaccinated, partially vaccinated or not
vaccinated at all according to the vaccine delivery strategy.
2. Number and percent of vaccinated girls experiencing serious adverse events, as
reported spontaneously through routine mechanisms of the UIP program;
3. Number and percent of vaccinated girls experiencing non-serious adverse events, as
reported spontaneously through routine mechanisms of the UIP program;
4. Timeliness of reporting serious adverse events to local, state and national authorities,
as per the usual UIP protocol; and
5. Timeliness of reporting non-serious adverse events to local, state and national
authorities, as per the usual UIP protocol.

9
Thus, the PATH study falls under the category of Post Marketing Trial (Phase IV) as per
Schedule Y .
Observation/Recommendation
2.17 The Committee in this regard took note of the expert opinion given in the Inquiry
Committee report which questioned the PATH description of the project and observed that since
“the demonstration project is a study of a pharmaceutical product carried out on humans and since
the primary objectives include the study of serious adverse effects, it is clear that clinical trial rules
and guidelines should apply”. (Para 2.3)
2.18 In fact, the Inquiry Committee in one of its findings very pointedly stated that the
investigators had variously labeled the research project carried out by them as “Observational
Study/Demonstrational Study,” etc. to establish that the study was not a clinical trial. But, since
the project had been carried out as research on human participants, it had to follow all the
guidelines and statutory requirements applicable for research on human participants. (Para 2.4)
Reply of the Ministry
2.19 The Inquiry Committee under the chairmanship of Prof SS Agarwal was of the opinion that
by whatever name it is called, the project proposal had been carried out as research on human
participants. As such, it had to follow all guidelines and statutory requirements applicable to
research on human participants.

V. MARKETING APPROVAL TO HPV V ACCINES IN INDIA
Observation/Recommendation
2.33 Before approving any new drug (including new vaccines), under Drugs and Cosmetics

Gardasil (Merck): Clinical trials were conducted on 108 subjects (girls in the age group of

investigations into the causes of deaths took an unacceptably long time. A number of discrepancies
and gaps in the investigations of the deaths have also been pointed out. There was no diary card
based reporting of adverse events for recording minor or major adverse events in the study
protocol in such a large study. This resulted in gross under reporting of the adverse events.
(Para 6.19)

has observed after reviewing all seven deaths (five deaths from AP in the Gardasil group and two
deaths in Gujarat from Cervarix group), that there was no common pattern to the deaths that
would suggest that these were caused by the vaccine. However, the reporting system as per
Government of India surveillance of vaccine preventable disease guidelines notification was not
done within time limit in two cases in AP and both the cases in Gujarat. There was no uniformity
in the reporting system of AEFI in both the States. The primary end point of the study was to
find out the number of girls having serious and no serious adverse events following vaccination
through routine UIP system. He has opined that in this regard first of all routine system of
reporting should have been verified in both States. (Para 6.20)

investigations of deaths could have been due to sole dependence on routine UIP protocol. It was a
significant lapse in the protocol and execution of the study. While reporting on safety aspects in the
study, it has been pointed out tr at there was absence of preparedness to handle Serious Adverse Events
(SAE) like anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, seizures, etc. occurring at the sites of vaccine administration.
Though such serious adverse events might be rare but it was advisable to be well prepared for such
an eventuality through adequate training of health workers. Assessment of the immune status of the
participants by the ANM, ASHA or the health workers was virtually nonexistent. These issues needed
to be addressed as prescribing information of the HPV vaccines specifically contra-ind1cates
administration in immune-compromised subjects (such as HIV/AIDS etc.). (Para 6.21)
2.53 The Committee, in the light of the observations made by experts, feels that the methodology
and implementation of the study at both the places was full of flaws. The Committee is of the view
that since the population under study was vulnerable, utmost caution should have been exercised
in the implementation of the study. The Committee also recommends that there should be an
independent monitoring mechanism in such a study involving human participants so that the
accurate recording of AEs and SAEs could be made. The findings of the experts clearly indicate
that the safety and rights of the children in this vaccination project were highly compromised and
violated. The Committee is also concerned over the fact that there was no insurance cover for the

II. NATURE OF PROJECT
Observation/Recommendation
4.1 The Committee finds the entire matter very intriguing and fishy. The choice of countries
and population groups; the monopolistic nature, at that point of time, of the product being pushed;
the unlimited market potential and opportunities in the universal immunization programmes of the
respective countries are all pointers to a well planned scheme to commercially exploit a situation.
Had PATH been successful in getting the HPV vaccine included in the universal immunization
programme of the concerned countries, this would have generated windfall profit for the
manufacturer(s) by way of automatic sale, year after year, without any promotional or marketing
expenses. It is well known that once introduced into the immunization programme it becomes
politically impossible to stop any vaccination. To achieve this end effortlessly without going through
the arduous and strictly regulated route of clinical trials, PATH resorted to an element of subterfuge
by calling the clinical trials as “Observational Studies” or “Demonstration Project” and various such
expressions. Thus, the interest, safety and well being of subjects were completely jeopardized by
PATH by using self-determined and self servicing nomenclature which is not only highly deplorable
but a serious breach of law of the land. The Committee is not aware about the strategy followed
by PATH in the remaining three countries viz. Uganda, Vietnam and Peru.
4.2 The Government should take up the matter with the Governments of these countries
through diplomatic channels to know the truth of the matter and take appropriate necessary action,
accordingly. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the responses of these countries in
the matter. (Para 2.5)
Reply of the Ministry

study by PATH. The gist of the same is as under:
● Consent forms and the actual implementation of the consent process.
● Method of monitoring the adverse effects and the serious adverse effects and remedial
measures for such events.
● Inclusion of vulnerable tribal population groups.
● Blurring of distinction between national Immunization Programme and PATH study.
● Insurance coverage for the study participants
● Free supply of vaccine by the manufacturer and the statement in the consent forms
that “you will not be charged for your daughter to receive the vaccine” that could be
considered as covert inducement and indirect coercion.

4.7 Obtaining Informed Consent from study subjects is a core requirement in the conduct of
clinical trials and protection of human rights. In case of minors, the Consent has to be signed by
parents/guardians. In the case of uneducated signatories, an independent person has to explain and
witness the consent process. The Informed Consent document approved by various Ethics
Committees on PATH project included the sentence: “I have read the information in this consent
form (or it has been read to me). I consent to allow my daughter to receive three doses of HPV
vaccines.” In the case of Andhra Pradesh 9,543 forms were signed, 1,948 had thumb impressions
while hostel warden had signed 2,763 forms. In the case of Gujarat 6,217 forms were signed,
3,944 had thumb impressions and 545 were either signed or carried thumb impression of guardians.
The data shows that a very large number of parents/guardians were illiterate and could not even
sign in their local language i.e. Telugu or Gujarati . (Para 6.12)
