AYUSH
I.         INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy which was set up by the Government of India
as an independent department in March, 1995, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare was renamed as
Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) in November, 2003.   The
main objective of the Department is to provide focused attention for the proper development and propagation of
Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and to fully utilize the potentials of these systems.
1.2       Thrust areas of the Department are: -
i)
                    Improvement and up-gradation of standards of education in AYUSH;
ii)                   Quality Control and Standardization of drugs;
iii)                 Ensuring sustained availability of raw materials, i.e. medicinal plants, metals, minerals and materials of
animal origin etc;
iv)                 Research & Development on the efficacy of the systems;
v)                  Participation of AYUSH in the National Health Care Delivery System & National Health & Family Welfare
Programme;
vi)                 Information, Education and Communication.
 
1.3       Over the years, there has been a steady growth in infrastructure of AYUSH.   At present, number of practitioners
of AYUSH in the country is 6,95,024.   There are 549 teaching institutions which include 454 Undergraduate colleges
and 95 Post-Graduate colleges.   Number of drug manufacturing units both in Govt. and private sector in the country is
9257.    There are 3100 Hospitals and 20811 dispensaries in the Govt. sector out of which maximum number of
hospitals and dispensaries provide Ayurvedic system of treatment.  Total number of Ayurveda Hospitals in the country
are 2253 and number of dispensaries in the                  country is 13925.
 
1.4       The Secretary, during the course of her presentation before the Committee, stated that the Department received
actual visibility during the Tenth Plan with the introduction of a number of Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored
Schemes aimed at development of educational institutions, research and quality control, hospitals and dispensaries etc. 
Achievements made during the year 2004-05 included establishment of ISMH wings in 23 district hospitals, 8 speciality
clinics/polyclinics, supply of essential drugs to 8152 AYUSH dispensaries in rural and backward areas, improvement of
educational infrastructure in respect of 120 educational institutions of AYUSH in the country. The Committee was also
informed that the only public sector undertaking of the Department i.e. the Indian Medicines Pharmaceutical
Corporation Limited (IMPCL), Mohan, Uttaranchal enhanced its turnover from about Rs. 3.35 crores in 2002-03 to Rs.
6.00 crores in 2004-05.   The Secretary pointed out that as a result of various activities undertaken during the year,
entire plan allocation of Rs. 200.00 crores for the year 2004-05 was utilised.

II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
2.1       The Plan Allocation of the Department for the year 2005-06 is Rs. 350.00 crore including Rs. 5.00 crore for the
Department of Urban Development for the completion of building for Pharmacopoeial Laboratory of Indian Medicine
(PLIM) and Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeial Laboratory (HPL).   Non-Plan allocation of the Department for 2005-06 is
Rs. 60.98 crore.  Whereas Plan allocation for 2005-06 has been substantially enhanced when compared with RE 2004-
05 allocation of   Rs. 200 crores, non-Plan allocation for 2005-06 does not reflect any increase. 
 
2.2       The Committee was informed that during the first two years of Tenth Plan, allocation of Rs. 150 crores in each
year remained underutilized due to various reasons.  The two main reasons were delay in approval of some centrally
sponsored schemes and lack of awareness among the implementing agencies about the schemes.  The Plan allocation of
the Department during the year 2004-05 was Rs.173.00 crore (excluding Rs. 8.00 crore for the Department of Urban
Development). Considering the performance of the Department and increased requirements of funds to implement
various Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes.  BE allocation was raised to Rs. 200.00 crore at RE Stage.  
Expenditure reported upto 28
th March, 2005 is Rs. 195.26 crore.  
 
2.3       The Committee was given to understand that an enhanced provision has been made  for 2005-06, in view of
genuine requirements of the Department under the various on-going programmes and its capacity  to utilize the
proposed provisions.   
The Department was confident of spending the increased budget provisions in 2005-06 as the Centrally Sponsored
Schemes under implementation are fully subscribed.  The Department was rather facing paucity of budget provisions in
implementing even feasible proposals under some of the schemes.
 
2.4       The Committee notes that against an allocation of Rs. 364.43 crore during the Ninth Plan, funds amounting to
only Rs. 293.72 crore could be utilised.   An enhanced allocation of Rs. 775 crore has been made for the Tenth Plan. 
The Committee notes that although utilisation position of allocated funds in the first year of the Tenth Plan i.e. 2002-03
was not satisfactory,  during the  second year,  the Department could utilise the entire allocation provided at the RE
stage.   For 2004-05, provision of Rs. 173 crore was enhanced to Rs. 200 crore.   The Department justified this enhanced
allocation by utilizing Rs. 195.26 crore by 28
th March, 2005. 
 
2.5       The Committee notes with satisfaction that with the increase in allocation, capacity of the Department to utilise
the same is also increasing.  The Committee would, however, like to point out that trend of utilisation is not evenly
spread in all the quarters of the financial year of 2004-05.   Against plan allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore in 2004-05, the
Department could utilise Rs. 121.33 crore  by the end of third quarter, i.e. 31st December, 2005.  By 7th March, 2005   it
increased to Rs. 179.49 crore and by the 28 th March, 05, utilisation figures were Rs. 195.26 crore.   This clearly shows
that out of total allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore in 2004-05, an expenditure of RS. 74.00 crore was made in the last

9th Report of Committee on Health & Family Welfare

quarter of the year.  The Committee is of the view that the pace of utilisation should be as per the prescribed financial
norms.   Expenditure on the high side in the last quarter of the financial year cannot be considered good for the health of
budget planning.  
 
2.6       The Committee is not fully convinced by the Department’s contention that there was full utilisation of the
allocated funds during   2004-05.   The Committee is constrained to observe that there are many schemes, both in central
sector and centrally sponsored whereunder funds remained underutilized.   Performance of some major schemes is self

2.7       The Committee, accordingly, requests that the Department should make concerted efforts for optimum and

III STATUTORY INSTITUTIONS
3.1       Central Council of Indian Medicine and Central Council of Homoeopathy are two Statutory Bodies constituted
under the Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 1970 and Homoeopathy Central Council Act, 1973 respectively.  The
main objective of these two statutory bodies is to regulate the medical     education in Indian Medicine and
Homoeopathy.
 
3.2       Initial allocation for Ninth Plan for the two Councils was Rs. 2.46 crores,  which by the end of the plan period
was brought down to Rs. 1.47 crores.  The Committee observes that whereas CCIM, New Delhi could utilise the
reduced allocation for the Ninth Plan, in the case of CCH, New Delhi, expenditure was restricted to only Rs. 2 lakhs
during the entire Ninth Plan and even this amount was spent during 1998-99.  The Committee observes that situation
remained the same during the Tenth Plan also.   During the       first two years, i.e 2002-03 and 2003-04 only a token
amount of Rs. 1 lakh was kept for CCH, New Delhi which remained  unspent.  During 2004-05 BE allocation of Rs. 1

9th Report of Committee on Health & Family Welfare
file:///D/health_family/9th%20Report.htm[29-06-2016 14:41:58]
lakh was increased to Rs. 10 lakhs.   This money was to be used for conducting workshops and meetings which failed to
materialize.  
 
3.3       In contrast, in the case of CCIM, there has been optimum utilisation of  allocated funds varying from Rs. 10 to
12 lakhs during this period.   The Committee also notes that CCH, New Delhi has been   utilizing the non-plan funds
fully which are on the same scale as provided to CCIM, New Delhi.   The Committee fails to understand the rationale
for variation in the provision of plan funds to both the Councils which have been set up with similar objectives. 
 
3.4       The Committee would like to be enlightened in this regard.  Committee’s attention has also been drawn by
provision of Rs. 20 lakhs in 2003-04 for conducting elections of CCH which remained unutilized due to the fact that
elections could not be conducted.  Provision was there for this purpose in 2002-03 also.  These elections seem to have
been finally conducted during the year 2004-05 as the provision meant for this purpose has been utilised.  The
Committee would like to know as to whether both these  statutory bodies are duly constituted with full membership.
 
3 .5      Maintenance of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy and revision thereof is another vital
objective which has to be carried out by the Councils on regular basis.   The Committee, however, finds that in the case
of CCIM, during 2004-05, Central Register of Delhi and Tamil Nadu was updated upto March, 2001 and  in the case of
Orissa and Rajasthan upto March, 2002.   The Committee fails to understand the factors responsible for the Central
Register of Indian Medicine  not being updated.   The Committee would like to be apprised about the position in respect
of other States.  The Committee would also like to have an idea about the status of the Central Register being
maintained by the Central Council of Homoeopathy.
 
3.6       The Committee has been given to understand that as on 1.1.2002, there are 6,91,470 AYUSH doctors which
include both Institutionally qualified and non-institutionally qualified doctors in the country, out of which maximum
number of AYUSH doctors i.e.  1,61,010 doctors are in Bihar.  The number of AYUSH doctors must have increased 
manifold in the last three years.  Prescribing standards of professional conduct, etiquette and code of  ethics to be
observed by the AYUSH doctors is another important mandate of the two Councils.   The Committee has been
observing that at present   there is no check on the AYUSH doctors practising which include both qualified doctors and
quacks.  The Committee is of the view that there needs to be an effective monitoring mechanism for regulating the
AYUSH doctors practising across the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that immediate action is
required to be taken either by the two councils or any other body which is empowered to regulate in such matters.
 
IV.       CENTRAL PHARMACY COUNCIL FOR AYUSH
4.1       The Committee has been commenting on no action being taken in the setting up of Central Pharmacy Council
for AYUSH for the last many years. Committee has observed that during 2002-03 token allocations was made for two
pharmacy councils   i.e. Indian Homeopathy Pharmacy Council and ISM Pharmacy Council.  However, in the next year 

9th Report of Committee on Health & Family Welfare
file:///D/health_family/9th%20Report.htm[29-06-2016 14:41:58]
it was decided to have one Pharmacy Council and accordingly Rs. 19 lakh  were provided therefor.  The money
allocated remained unspent as the Bill was yet to be finalized.   The Committee is constrained to observe that during
2004-05 also, position remained the same.  The Committee finds that during 2005-06 Rs. 1 crore has been provided for
the proposed Council.  The Department has informed that  the Bill has been prepared and the comments of the
Ministries of Finance, HRD and Health & Family Welfare  obtained.   The draft Bill is almost ready and will be
introduced in Parliament shortly.  The Committee reiterates that there should be no further delay for introducing the Bill
in Parliament. 
 
V. HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
Advanced Ayurvedic Centre  for Mental Health in NIMHANS
5.1       An Advanced Ayurvedic Centre for Mental Health was proposed to be set up in NIMHANS, Bangalore. 
Accordingly Rs. 1.45 crore were provided in Ninth Plan.  The Committee observes that although Rs. 97 lakhs were
spent during the Ninth Plan period, nothing seems to have materialized in the operationalisation of the centre.  The
Committee has to make such a comment only because of trend of expenditure in the three years of the Tenth Plan.  Rs.
26 lakhs were provided in 2002-03 but the allocated funds remained unutilized.    There was no provision during 2003-
04.  However, in 2004-05 Rs. 1 lakh has been provided for this Centre.  The Committee strongly feels that any
scheme/plan proposed to be implemented should only be taken up after due consideration of its feasibility and other
allied aspects.  Advanced Ayurvedic Centre for Mental Health in NIMHANS, Bangalore seems to have been forsaken
by the Department.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the actual status of this Centre.   
 
VI.       RESEARCH COUNCILS (INTRA & EXTRA ) MURAL RESEARCH
6.1       The Central Council  for Research in Ayurveda and Siddha (CCRAS) , an autonomous organization set up in
1978 has the mandate to initiate, aid, guide, develop and co-ordinate scientific research in different aspects of Ayurveda
and Siddha.  The Committee notes that the Council has made optimum and judicious allocated funds during the Ninth
Plan.  Tenth Plan allocation of Rs. 45 crores for the Council is on a higher side when compared with Ninth Plan
allocation of Rs. 35.62 crore. Like Ninth plan, during the first three years of Tenth Plan also, the Council has managed
to utilize allocated fund fully.  However, the Committee finds that during 2004-05 the Physical Targets set for different

6.2       The Committee observes that during 2004-05 physical targets could not be achieved fully inspite of there being
full utilisation of funds.  Plan allocation for 2005-06 stands at Rs. 12.50 crore which is higher than Rs. 8 crore provided
in 2004-05.  The Committee would like to emphasize that all required steps should be taken for achieving the physical

VII.     CENTRAL COUNCIL FOR RESEARCH INSTITUTE OF UNANI MEDICINE, NEW DELHI
7.1       The Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine, a registered society set up in 1978 has a network of 24
centres functioning in different parts of the country for developing and coordinating scientific research on different
aspects of Unani Medicine.  The trend of utilisation of funds during the first three years of Tenth Plan indicates that
additional funds are being provided at R.E stage for carrying out the Construction Work of Regional Research Institute
of Unani Medicine, Srinagar.  The Committee observes that during 2004-05, Plan allocation enhanced from Rs. 9.50
crore to Rs. 13.50 crore at the R. E stage.  This additional provision was also meant for construction of 2
nd phase of the
building of RRUM Srinagar.  The Committee has been given to understand that these funds were to be provided to the
construction wing of the Kashmir University which is constructing the building.  The Committee finds that 2004-05 also
an enhanced provision of Rs. 11.50 crore has been proposed. The Committee would like to be apprised about the
specific purpose for which this additional allocation is meant for.  The Committee would also like to point out that the
construction of building for RRUM has been continuing for about 8-10 years.  The Committee would like to be
enlightened about the original estimate and the actual expenditure on this construction project.
 
VIII. CENTRAL COUNCIL OF RESEARCH IN HOMEOPATHY
8.1       The Council is an autonomous body set up in 1978 with the objective of formulation of patterns of research on
scientific lines in Homeopathy etc. The Council functions through the Network of 2 CRIs, 1 HDRI, 7 RRIs and 23
Research Units spread all over the country.  Against Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 16.94 crore, an enhanced provision of
Rs. 22 crore has been made for the Council.  The Committee, however, finds that during the first three years of Tenth
Plan Rs. 14 crore have been provided for.  The actual expenditure is Rs. 16.27 crore by making additional allocation at
RE stage.  The provision for 2005-06 is Rs. 11 crore.  This means that entire allocation during Tenth Plan has been
accounted for.  The Committee has been given to understand that during 2004-05 due to setting up of Regional Research
Institute at Guwahati and Noida additional funds had to be provided at RE stage.  The Committee would like to have an
idea of quantum of funds spent on construction activities during the first three years of Tenth Plan.  The Committee
would also like to know about the status of all the research Institutes functioning under CCRA.

Govt./Government/Universities/NGOs.) etc.

9.1       The Tenth Plan allocation for Extra Mural projects is Rs. 10 crores. Similar provision was also made in the Ninth
Plan. However, funds amounting to only Rs. 4.15 crore could be utilised.  During the Tenth Plan Rs. 3.19 crore have
been utilised during the first three years.  The Committee notes that for 2005-06, Rs. 15 crore have been provided
whereas, the entire allocation is only Rs. 10 crore.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the reason for this
trend of allocation.  9.2            The Committee observes that research projects are being implemented by different
agencies.  The Committee would like to have a status note on the contributions made  in this sector.  One of the
important mandated activities under this Head is to assist research projects and interventions which validate efficacy
claims relating to AYUSH.  An idea about the achievements made in this regard may be given. 
 
X.        SURVEY ON “USAGE & ACCEPTABILITY OF AYUSH
10.1     During the Ninth Plan, there was a provision of Rs. 81 lakhs for conducting a survey on Usage and Acceptability
of AYUSH against which expenditure incurred was   Rs. 46 lakhs.  Tenth Plan provision for this purpose is Rs. 1 crore. 
The Committee finds that during the first year no progress could be made due to delay in finalization of survey agency. 
During the next year i.e. 2003-04, allocated funds of Rs. 12 lakhs had to be reduced to Rs. 6 Lakhs at RE stage due to
delay in the finalization of the survey instruments. The Committee finds that the Plan allocation of Rs. 5.70 Lakhs for
2004-05 also remained under utilised. 
10.2     As per the Annual Report 2004-05 of the Department, a survey was conducted with the help of ICMR, with the
main objective to collect information on availability   of facilities in the hospitals and dispensaries under AYUSH and
the extent of utilization of these services in treatment of the diseases by the population alongwith the various problems
being faced by the AYUSH systems/AYUSH practitioners in practising these systems.  The report of the survey has
been finalized and submitted to the Department.
10.3     As per the report, for 35 districts as a whole, ISM&H was preferred by one-third of the surveyed house holds, in
cases of normal ailments and by about 18% in cases of serious ailments and 14% of the sick persons as a whole, availed
ISM&H systems for treatment of their illness. 
10.4     The Committee observes that undue delay has taken place in conducting the survey on usage and acceptability of
AYUSH.  The Committee is perturbed to note that the although funds were available, considerable time was taken in
deciding the survey agency and other allied matters.  It has taken the entire Ninth Plan and more than half of Tenth Plan
for conducting of survey which is very vital for propogating AYUSH.  The findings of the survey confirms the
apprehensions of the Committee about the lack of publicity and resultant lack of demand for AYUSH in the general
public in the country.  The Committee would appreciate if there is no delay in taking follow up action on the findings of
the survey and the Department should initiate the remedial measures at the earliest.
 
10.5     The Committee has been informed that another survey has been assigned to ICMR to collect information on the
level of acceptability and non-acceptability of AYUSH from the patients attending the CGHS dispensaries. The survey
also proposes to cover the patients from the teaching hospitals attached to AYUSH Colleges located in the 15 cities

during this plan period.  The first two years of the Tenth Plan were taken in deciding about the Government share,
whether to establish it as a joint venture with a private party or not and also obtaining the approval of the Ministry of

12.1     This is a new scheme started in 2003-04 for providing benefits of AYUSH system to CGHS beneficiaries.  In its

observes that situation remained unchanged during 2004-05.  It has been informed that dispensaries opened in the year
2003-04 have started functioning and seven more dispensaries have been sanctioned during 2004-05.  The Committee
is, however, surprised to note that physical targets set during both the years i.e. 2003-04 remained unfulfilled.  Not even
one dispensary sanctioned in 2003-04 has become functional.   The Committee does not have any hope for the seven
dispensaries sanctioned  in 2004-05.   This is  born out by     the fact that allocated funds for the scheme remained
unutilized during 2003-04 and 2004-05.   The Committee is of the view that there is a little chance of AYUSH
dispensaries sanctioned becoming functional.   The Department has itself conceded that there are large number of
vacancies in AYUSH dispensaries. The Committee is not convinced by the contention of the Department that the
process of new recruitment is to be taken up by the UPSC and revival of old posts is complicated and time
consuming.The Committee is of the view that when the existing CGHS dispensaries are not fully functional for
lack of AYUSH manpower, fate of AYUSH dispensaries proposed to be opened can be well imagined.

XV. STRENGTHENING OF PHARMACOPOEIAL LABORATORIES
15.1     Pharmacopoeial Laboratory for Indian Medicine and Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeial Laboratory were
established in Ghaziabad in 1970s with the objective of laying down the standards for drugs of AYUSH and also for
their testing/analysis. 
15.2     The Committee has been observing that both the labs lack required infrastructure including staff.  The
Committee observes that during the Tenth Plan Period, funds are being allocated every year to be reduced drastically at
the RE stage, specially in the case of PLIM.  The only reason cited being non-creation of posts. The status  of these labs
remains unchanged  for the last so many years.  Year 2004-05 was no exception.  Rs. 55 lakhs were provided for PLIM,
to be reduced to Rs. 9 lakhs at the RE stage  and the actual expenditure upto 7
th March,2005 was only Rs.4.77 lakhs.
Reason given is non-creation of posts. For strengthening of these two labs, plan allocation proposed for 2005-06 is Rs.
150.00 lakhs. The Committee, however, strongly feels that higher allocation of funds does not have any meaning
in the case of these labs. Lack of infrastructure is adversely affecting the achievement level of various physical
targets set by the two labs.
 
15.3     The Committee notes that out of 36 sanctioned posts in PLIM and 32 in HPL, only 2 and 3 posts are lying vacant
respectively. However, this strength must be based on the initial year of establishment of these two labs i.e in the 1970s. 
Since then, after more than 30 years, the  requirement of posts must have increased manifold. The Department itself has
mentioned that additional 53 posts are required in PLIM and 31 in HPL. As per the latest information given by the
Department, for the first phase of strengthening the requirement of labs, 16 and 19 posts were projected for PLIM and
HPL respectively. The matter is under the consideration of the Department of Expenditure.
 
15.4     The Committee is anguished to note that another plan period would be over and these two labs will
continue to suffer from lack of required staff. The Committee finds that PLIM continues to function without a
Director. Nothing can be more unsatisfactory. In view of a very large variety of AYUSH drugs in the open
market, these labs have to be fully operational. The Committee reiterates that the Department should vigorously
purpose the matter with the Ministry of Finance and other authorities.            
 
15.5     The Committee was given to understand that buildings for HPL and PLIM are expected to be ready by February,
2005. However, as per the latest information, the buildings of HPL and PLIM will be ready by June, 2005 and July,
2005 respectively. The Committee hopes that there would be no further delay due to formal clearance by Fire
Department and other allied agencies.

has also taken a number of steps which include central assistance for strengthening of 21 drug testing labs of AYUSH
system, for GMP compliance, for appointment of drug controllers/drug inspectors.

medicines were analyzed.  Gujarat Govt.  has initiated action against one person for selling spurious Ayurvedic product. 
9 samples of fake homeopathic medicines were analyzed in Delhi.   The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction with
the scant feedback about spurious AYUSH drugs for such a big country and that too for a period of three years. 
The Committee would emphasize that the Department should pursue with all the departments so that
preventive/deterrent action can be initiated, wherever required.

XVII.   EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS
17.1    There are 221 Ayurveda Colleges and 180 Homoeopathy Colleges that have the approval of State Govts. and  are
by and large affiliated to the universities.   A state-wise breakup of these colleges indicates that the maximum number of
ayurveda colleges is concentrated in two states of Karnataka and Maharashtra.  Similarly in case of homoeopathy
colleges Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh have the highest number of colleges.   On being asked about the reasons for
this situation, the department clarified that this was largely due to the higher degree of private initiatives in these states. 
The Central Govt. has been taking all preventive measures to check the mushroom growth of sub-standard medical
institutions of ayurveda and homeopathy.   The Department has also informed that no college can be opened without a
NOC from the state govt. and consent of affiliation from the concerned university.  The Committee is not fully inclined
to accept the clarification given by the Department.  The Department itself has indicated that all these colleges are ‘by
and large’ affiliated to universities. 
 
17.2     The Committee also notes that number of govt. colleges are very less when compared with the private colleges.  
Out of 221 ayurveda colleges, only 54 are in the govt. sector.   Similarly, out of 180 homoeopathy colleges 149 are
private colleges.  This is the position in case of unani and siddha colleges.   The Committee has been informed that the
Central Council of Indian Medicine and the Central Council of Homeopathy made inspections of a number of colleges
during 2002-03 and 2003-04.    The Committee has been given to understand that the colleges found lacking facilities
for teaching and practical training were not allowed admission.   The inspection reports have been communicated to
such colleges for rectification of deficiencies.  The Committee would like to be enlightened about the follow up
action taken in this regard.

under the lump sum provision, action for clearance of all procedural formalities is required to be taken by the
Department. (Para 13.2) 
 
XIV. NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD

  The Committee expresses its serious concern over the tardy progress being made in providing the
required staff essential for its efficient functions.  The Committee fails to appreciate the proposal of the
Department of Expenditure of outsourcing of staff for the Board.  The Committee is of the view that there should
be creation of all required posts.  The Department should make concerted efforts for getting the EFC and
Cabinet approval for creation of required posts at the earliest. (Para 14.1) 
 
XV. STRENGTHENING OF PHARMACOPOEIAL LABORATORIES
The Committee, however, strongly feels that higher allocation of funds does not have any meaning in the
case of these labs. Lack of infrastructure is adversely affecting the achievement level of various physical targets
set by the two labs. (Para 15.2) 
 
15.4     The Committee is anguished to note that another plan period would be over and these two labs will
continue to suffer from lack of required staff. The Committee finds that PLIM continues to function without a
Director. Nothing can be more unsatisfactory. In view of a very large variety of AYUSH drugs in the open
market, these labs have to be fully operational. The Committee reiterates that the Department should vigorously
purpose the matter with the Ministry of Finance and other authorities. (Para 15.4)     
 
The Committee hopes that there would be no further delay due to formal clearance by Fire Department
and other allied agencies.     (Para 15.5)     
 
XVI.    DRUGS QUALITY CONTROL
 
The Committee is constrained to note that all the above schemes were proposed to be launched without going
into the feasibility aspect.  As a result, after three years two of the schemes had to be dropped.  One was transferred to
another scheme and two were merged with the main scheme of drug quality control.  It took 3 years to realize that the
subject of regulation of health food supplements belongs to the Department of Health as per the Allocation of Business
Rules.   Therefore, the Scheme of Health Food Supplements was transferred to the Department of Health. (Para 16.3)  
 
            The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction with the scant feedback about spurious AYUSH drugs for such a big
country and that too for a period of three years.  The Committee would emphasize that the Department should pursue
with all the departments so that preventive/deterrent action can be initiated, wherever required.  (Para 16.4 & 16.5)
 
The Committee would also like to recommend that if need be, this Cell may be strengthened and function as a 
nodal agency in the vital area of curbing of manufacture and sale of spurious AYUSH drugs. (Para 16.6)
 
The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by the Council and the Department.   The Committee, however, feels that
the Department should also inform the scientists of Harvard Medical School about the rationale for the presence of
metals in Ayurvedic drugs and their safety aspect.   (Para 16.7)
 
XVII.   EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS
The Committee would like to be enlightened about the follow up action taken in this regard. (Para 17.1 & 17.2)
 
XVIII. MISCELLANEOUS
The Committee is of the view that the Department should pursue this proposal with all concerned authorities. 
(Para 18.1)
 
The Committee feels that a decision in this matter should be taken after considering the views of all
stakeholders. (Para 18.2)
 
The Committee welcomes this ambitious partnership programme and hopes that research work to be undertaken
under this project will yield fruitful results for all concerned. (Para 18.4)

CHAPTER – I
RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE
GOVERNMENT HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II.  BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation (para 2.11)
1.1 The Committee is of the opinion that keeping in view the mandate of DHR/ICMR to bring
modern technologies to the people through research and innovations and the fact that Department
has just launched the above mentioned Schemes to fulfill its mandate of creating a strong and
effective eco-system for carrying out health research in the country and for introduction of new
technologies, new methods of treatment and products/processes into the public health system; any
underfunding to the schemes would prove detrimental in achieving the desired objectives that too
at a time when these schemes have just picked up their pace. In view of the fact that with this
funds crunch it would not be possible for the Department to roll out many of its proposed
initiatives under the schemes, the Committee recommends that the Department should vigorously
pursue with the Ministry of Finance for enhanced funds at RE Stage. The Committee,
simultaneously, also recommends to the Department that it should take all out efforts for optimum
and judicious utilization of available resources and funds for implementation of various Schemes.
Funds for new initiatives should be limited to availability of funds.
Action Taken
1.2 As recommended by the Committee, efforts will also be made by the Department for
optimum utilization of the available funds, by taking following actions:
(i) The Department would impress upon the Ministry of Finance for making enhanced
allocations of funds at the RE stage for meeting the targets of the various schemes
in 2015-16.
(ii) While funding of new initiatives, preference will be given to the research projects/
proposals on health issues of national and public health importance, like, Cancer,
Cardio-vascular diseases, Diabetes, Maternal and Child Health, Nutritional
Deficiencies, V ector Borne Diseases, TB, Leprosy and Blindness control.
(iii)  Monthly monitoring to review the physical and financial progress of the schemes
will be done at the level of Joint Secretary to ensure efficient and effective
utilisation of budgetary allocations.
(iv) Similar review and monitoring on periodic basis will be done at the level of
Secretary, DHR.
(v) Conducting field visits to the medical colleges and institutions for reviewing the
progress of implementation of the schemes and making rational assessment of
requirement of funds.
2

3
III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.6)
1.3 The Committee puts on record its appreciation for ICMR for near optimum utilization of
allocated funds. Such a trend of utilization by the Institute would strengthen its demand for
additional funds at RE stage during the current year, as per the projections made. However, the
Committee would also like to say that mere utilization of funds is not an indicator of success,
unless the research outcomes are translated into health products or are used in better interest of
people. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps being taken in speedy translation of
research leads into public utilities. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the number
of leads which were actually put into public use for their betterment.
Action Taken
1.4 The ICMR’s technologies/leads are shared with National Research Development Corporation
(NRDC) and Biotech Consortium India Limited (BCIL) under the Ministry of Science and
Technology, for technology transfer/commercialization.
1.5 The Division of Innovation & Translational Research (ITR) of ICMR is regularly following
up with the companies to review the progress. Through this process, eleven technologies have been
transferred to industries for commercialization.
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.11)
1.6 The Committee is happy to note that at its behest the Department has revisited its priorities
areas for research and drawn three most important priorities areas namely Cancer Research,
Environmental Health and Maternal and Child Health for carrying out research. The Committee is
hopeful that this move of the Department would result in visible and desirable results. The
Committee desires to be apprised of the outcome of the above move.
Action Taken
1.7 ICMR has constituted a core committee to develop cancer management guidelines of 20
specific types of cancers. Guidelines for 4 types of Cancers: Colorectal Cancer, Gall bladder
Cancer, Buccal Mucosa Cancer and Gastric cancer have been published and uploaded on the ICMR
website for public use. Guidelines for another 4 sites of cancers are in process of uploading on
the website.
1.8 ICMR has established the National Institute for Disease Informatics and Research, at
Bangalore for compiling the Cancer registries on national basis.
1.9 On the issues related to Environmental Health, ICMR has established the National Institute
for Research in Environmental Health (NIREH) at Bhopal.
1.10 On health issues related to air pollution, a Centre for Advanced Research has been
established in Chennai. The Centre has created a network of scientists across the country to
conduct research on households air pollution.
1.11 In the Maternal and Child Health (MCH), the priority areas of research are: reduction of
pre-natal and neonatal morbidities and mortalities; safe pregnancy and motherhood practices;

4
discovery of new, safe and acceptable contraception; reduction of respiratory (pneumonia) infection
in infants; polycystic ovarian syndrome diseases and better survival of low birth weight babies.
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.18)
1.12 The Committee appreciates the intervention made by the Department in the area of
environmental pollution and desires that research activities should not be restricted to air pollution
only as the health hazards of water/noise pollution are also affecting a large chunk of population.
Action Taken
1.13 Research activities of the National Institute of Occupational Health of ICMR, Ahmedabad
are not restricted to air pollution only and their thrust areas of research also include other
environmental hazards like, like noise pollution, water pollution thermal pollution and industrial
waste etc.

CHAPTER- II
RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF  THE GOVERNMENT REPLIES
III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.20)
2.1 During the presentation on ICMR, the Committee was apprised about the network of ICMR
Institutes/Centres spread across the country. On a perusal thereof, the Committee noted that there
are regional imbalances in the presence of ICMR across the country. The Committee noted that a
large area of the Central India which also  happened to be tribal area which is malaria infected and
affected with various other environment-related morbidity factors is not covered under the projects
on traditional medicines. The Committee, accordingly, recommends to the Department to pay
attention in those areas which are not well served and seek additional resources for Eastern India
and Central India.
Action Taken
2.2 In addition to the existing Institutes/Centres of ICMR, the Department will be implementing
the 5 new schemes, viz. (1) Establishment of Multi-Disciplinary Research Units in Government
Medical Colleges, (2) Establishment of Model Rural Health Research Units in the States, (3)
Establishment of a Network of Laboratories for Managing Epidemics and Natural Calamities,
(4) Human Resource Development for Health Research and (5) Grant-in-Aid for Inter-sector
Convergence & Coordination for Promotion & Guidance on Health Research, which will result in
the opening of new centres/laboratories in central and eastern India and unserved areas.
IV. PROGRAMMES FOR THE NORTH EAST (NE)
Recommendation/Observation (para 4.3)
2.3 From a perusal of the initiatives proposed for NE region in the year 2015-16 vis-a-vis those
taken in the year 2014-15, the Committee notes that nothing new region specific programme has
been envisaged for the current year. The actual expenditure incurred vis-a-vis allocations made in
the year 2014-15 is also not very promising and reflects that many of the proposed initiatives
visualized for the year perhaps were either delayed or not accomplished. The Committee hence
exhorts that the Department may take all measures for optimum and judicious utilization of the
allocations made in the current financial year for the NE region.
Action Taken
2.4 During the year 2015-16, priority will be given to release the next instalment in respect of
the Multi-Disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) Viral Diagnostic & Research Laboratories and Model
Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs) already sanctioned in the NE States.
Efforts will also be made to cover all the States/all the probable region in establishing the
Viral Diagnostic & Research Laboratories (VRDLs) and MRUs.
5

6
2.5 The following activities are also proposed in the North Eastern Region during  2015-16:
Bio medical Research Centre (BRC) of ICMR at Hengrabari, Guwahati is to be
constructed with an estimated cost of R47.58 Crores.
A Field Station of Regional Medical Research Centre, Dibrugarh is to be
established at Agartala (Tripura). A land measuring 3 acres has been acquired for this
purpose.
A Memorandum of Understanding has been signed between ICMR and
Government of Arunachal Pradesh to establish a Multi-Disciplinary Research Unit of
ICMR in  the Arunachal State Hospital, Naharlagun.
Beside the above stated new activity, ICMR has established
Multi- disciplinary Research Units at Falkawn, Mizoram and Kohima, Nagaland in 2014-15.
2.6 ICMR is also focusing on research activities on communicable diseases in the North
Eastern Region. A total of 35 research projects have been shortlisted, out of which 6 projects have
been initiated and remaining are awaiting technical/financial approval. Two Task Force studies on
neonatal sepsis and transmission of malaria infection employing newer technology at international
border areas will also be initiated in 2015-16.
VI. DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PROMOTION OF HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 6.10)
2.7 The Committee desires that more States may be covered under the Scheme. The
Department may also set up more MRHRUs covering all the States.

th Five Year Plan to cover
more States, based on the outcomes and success of the programme in the already sanctioned
MRHRUs.

GUIDANCE ON HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 7.9)
2.9 The Committee apprehends that shortfall in allocations made for the Scheme would hamper
the pace of projects already initiated. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to
take all measures to offset impact of shortfall of allocations. Simultaneously, the Department
should also present a strong case for seeking more funds at RE Stage.

2.10 The Department would impress upon the Ministry of Finance for making enhanced
allocations of funds at the RE stage for meeting the targets of the various schemes in 2015-16.
2.11 As recommended by the Committee, efforts will also be made by the Department for
optimum utilization of the available funds to offset the impact of shortfall in allocations, by taking
following actions:

(i) priority will be given to meet the committed expenditure on the already sanctioned
projects/Units.
(ii) While funding of new initiatives, preference will be given to the research projects/
proposals on health issues of national & public health importance, like, Cancer,

be done at the level of Joint Secretary to ensure efficient and effective utilisation

progress of implementation of the schemes and making rational assessment of
requirement of funds.
(vi) Speedy release of grants to the medical colleges to improve the profile of utilisation

Recommendation/Observation (para 8.8)
2.12 The Committee is perturbed to find that the component for creation of the Revolving
fund to facilitate a rapid mobilization of outbreak/disaster response to infectious diseases
outbreak or a natural or man made disaster was not approved in the EFC meeting held under
the Chairmanship of Finance Secretary and Secretary of Expenditure. The Committee observes

diseases like Swine Flu, Chikunguniya etc. As the Department has also expressed its inability

CHAPTER – III
RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE
GOVERNMENT HA VE NOT  BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
Recommendation/Observation (para 2.3)
3.1 The Committee notes that on one hand the Department claims that significant progress has
been made in respect of Schemes while on the other the Committee notes that only a meagre
amount of expenditure of R179.36 crore upto 4.3.2015 could be made against the allocations of
R5213.00 crore made for the Schemes for Twelfth Plan Period. The Committee understands that
all the Schemes could be rolled in the year 2013-14 only and hence the expenditure booked was
very low. The Committee, however, is constrained to comment that this state of affairs indicates
that the Department was consistently over estimating its requirements and has not been able to
make use of scarce financial resources. The Committee, accordingly, impresses upon the
Department to make all out efforts to implement its proposed activities under the schemes in the
remaining two years of the Twelfth Five Year Plan for optimum utilization of allocations and for
achieving the desired objectives.
Action Taken
3.2 The Twelfth Plan allocation of R5213.00 crores for the five newly formulated schemes of
the DHR was based on the proposed estimated cost of each scheme. However, the final cost of
all the five schemes approved by the EFC/Cabinet worked out to be R3055.00 crores (approx.).
Against this, the actual budgetary allocation in the first four years (2012-13 to 2015-16) has been
to the extent of R677.00 crores only.
3.3 Allocation in 2012-13 for the schemes could not be utilised as the schemes could be finally
approved by the EFC/Cabinet in 2013-14. In fact, the two schemes, namely, (1) Human Resource
Development for Health Research and (2) Grant in aid scheme for Inter sectoral Convergence &
Promotion and guidance on Health Research were approved in February, 2014 only.
3.4 The Department has made its estimation meticulously at the time of finalization of Twelfth
Plan allocation for all the five schemes. However, while approving the schemes, the physical targets
were reduced, due to which the financial cost of the schemes came down from the original
proposed cost of R5213 crores to R3055 crores.
3.5 The schemes were rolled out for implementation immediately and the proposal were
processed for technical evaluation and final approval for release of fund in the same year. This was
possible only since pre-project actions had been taken by the Department in respect of all the five
schemes.
3.6 Depending upon the budgetary allocations, all efforts will be made by the Department to
implement the schemes by achieving maximum physical targets, through optimum utilization of
allocated resources.
8

9
Further Recommendation
3.7 The Committee does not find plausible the explanation given by the Department on
the formulation and approved procedure for the five schemes. Either the Department lacks
serious wherewithal to ensure timely formulation or approval of schemes or does not have
the vision to plan and implement schemes. The Committee seriously doubts whether these
schemes would be taken to their logical conclusion at the end of the Twelfth Five Year Plan
keeping in view the physical and financial progress made so far. The Committee, once again
recommends that the Department should identify and overcome the shortcomings in the
mechanism of budgetary planning so that the under-utilization of budgeted funds being
witnessed do not recur in the remaining years of the Twelfth Plan and the desired objectives
are not compromised.
Recommendation/Observation (para 2.6)
3.8 As evident from the above tables there are huge variations between the BE and RE for all
the schemes as well as for ICMR. The reasons cited by the Department for this trend were non-
receipt of adequate number of applications on account of approval of the scheme at fag end of
2013-14, pendency of utilization certificates, receipt of less number of proposals from States and
non-completion of requisite administrative and technical formalities under the Schemes guidelines by
certain States. The Committee, in the circumstances, is constrained to observe that inspite of its
repeated recommendations to the Department to take all out measures, including completion of pre-
project planning and formalities of obtaining necessary approvals for optimum and judicious
utilization of budgeted funds, not much has been done in this regard. The Committee fails to
understand the reasons for the delay in formulation of all the schemes even though the Schemes
first got in- principle approval by the Planning Commission in December 2010. The Committee is
not convinced with the statement of the Department that inspite of its best efforts, the various
actions like the appraisal of the Schemes, responding to various appraisal agencies, clearance of
the Schemes by EFC/CCEA took more than anticipated time which ultimately led to the delay. The
Committee observes that this is a clear case of lack of foresight and faulty planning by the
Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make all possible
efforts with proper and timely planning to utilize the allocated funds at BE Stage. The Committee
would like to be apprised of the steps being taken or proposed to be taken to arrest this trend of
underutilization of budgeted funds which eventually led to massive cuts at RE stage.
Action Taken
3.9 The in-principle  approval of the Planning Commission to the Schemes was received in
December, 2010 i.e. in the midst of Eleventh Five Year Plan. The detailed EFC documents were
prepared and circulated by the Department for the comments of the appraisal agencies, soon
thereafter. However, since 2011-12 was the last year of the Eleventh Five Year Plan, the
Department was advised to formulate comprehensive schemes for the full Twelfth Plan period.
3.10 Hence, revision of EFC documents with modified cost estimates for the Twelfth plan period
and the process of obtaining approvals from the EFC and Cabinet took time and the schemes could
be finally approved in 2013-14 only.

10
3.11 The Department had already taken advance actions for inviting proposals from the States/
Medical Colleges, etc. and it was as a result of this action that it was possible to roll out and
implement all the five schemes during 2013-14 itself, alongwith the release of funds for the various
projects.
3.12 W ith a view to ensure optimum utilisation of allocated funds under the various schemes,
regular monitoring of physical/financial progress of the projects is being made through periodical
progress reports as well as  through onsite visits by the teams from DHR/ICMR. Review meetings
are also held at the level of Joint Secretary and Secretary (DHR) and action plan is formulated for
effective implementation of all the schemes and for utilisation of allocated funds.
Further Recommendation
3.13 The Committee would like to be apprised of the progress made in the actual
implementation of these five schemes and whether the intended objectives of the five
schemes would be achieved by end of the Twelfth Plan.
V . HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT FOR HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 5.6)
3.14 The Committee fails to understand as to why there was so much delay in implementing the
scheme which resulted in surrender of the entire budgeted funds for the year 2012-13 and drastic
reduction of allocations in RE 2013-14. Trained and qualified manpower is pre-requisite for
implementation of various research schemes of the Department. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department must complete all pre-project activities timely and properly to
avoid recurrence of the existing trend of underutilization. Allocation may be increased at RE stage,
if necessary, depending on the number of eligible proposals received. Publicity may be given to the
Scheme.
Action Taken
3.15 (1) Additional allocations, if considered necessary, will be sought at RE stage, depending
upon the number of applications for fellowships received and found edible for funding,
(2) The steps taken to improve the utilization of funds under the scheme include the following:
(i)  Letter has been addressed to the Principal Secretaries of Health & Family Welfare and
Directors of Medical Education of the States/UT, for giving wide publicity to the
scheme to attract adequate number of applications.
(ii) DHR will also give wide publicity through newspapers/websites for inviting applications.
3.16 The medical colleges/institutions will be impressed upon during various review meetings and
field visits by the officers to motivate the factually/researchers to avail the facilities under the
scheme.
Further Recommendation
3.17 The Committee recommends that this scheme should be given maximum importance
by the Department and would like to be apprised of the actual steps taken on ground to
enhance Human Resource Development for Health Research as Human Resource

11
Development is a key pillar for implementation of advances to be made in Health Research
which would in turn ensure incremental innovations to curb the various diseases plaguing
the country and also help in reducing costs for implementation of various Health
Programmes optimally.
VI. DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PROMOTION OF HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 6.6)
3.18 The Committee observes that deaths caused due to non-communicable diseases are much
more than those occurring due to communicable diseases and any underfunding to the Scheme,
which promotes research in Non-Communicable diseases, will prove detrimental to control lifestyle
diseases. The proposed shortfall in allocation to the Scheme may lead to curtailment in the second
or subsequent installments to the Institutes where the Department has already made a beginning and
would result in seriously hampering of research activities initiated. The Committee, therefore, lends
its support to the demand of the Department for enhancement of allocations at RE Stage for the
Scheme so that investments already made in the medical colleges under the Scheme do not go
down the drain. The Committee finds that life style-related disease like hypertension, blood
pressure, diabetes etc. are on the rise and are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the
country and, therefore, it is a cause of serious concern. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the life style-related diseases may be included in the research programmes of the Department.
Action Taken
3.19 ICMR and the Medical Colleges will be requested to include life-style related diseases,
namely, diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular diseases, in their research programmes.
Further Recommendation
3.20 The Committee would like to be apprised of the specific steps taken by ICMR to
include lifestyle diseases in their research programmes.
VII. GRANT-IN-AID FOR INTER-SECT ORAL CONVERGENCE & PROMOTION AND
GUIDANCE ON HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 7.8)
3.21 The Committee observes that some of very important activities are targeted to be
accomplished under the Scheme for Inter-Sectoral Convergence & Promotion and Guidance on
Health Research. The Committee is happy to note that pursuant to its recommendation made in 56th
Report and reiterated in 67th Report for creation of an institutional coordination mechanism for
synergizing the core competencies of the different organizations/agencies a group of Secretaries has
been constituted, consisting of Secretaries from DBT, DRDO, DARE/ICAR, ISRO, Department of
Space, DIT etc. to coordinate and collaborate on Health Research activities among various
departments. The Committee hopes that anticipated dividends are being accrued from this move.
Action Taken
3.22 In pursuance of the meeting of the Steering Committee of the Group of Secretaries (GoS)
held on 21st January 2014  and the Review Meeting of the Working Groups held on 12.08.2014

12
under the chairmanship of Secretary-Department of Health Research & DG (ICMR), following 10
priority areas have been  identified for undertaking joint research projects:

(ii) Use of Traditional Systems of Medicine in Maternal & Child Health care

(vii) Public Health in Emergencies/Disasters

(ix) Human Nutrition with a priority on Food Safety, Agricultural Instrumentation &

(x) Standardization of Treatment Procedures under Rashtriya Swasth Bima Yojana
(RSBY)
3.23 The concerned lead departments are required to take further actions for developing the joint
research projects in consultation with the other member departments.
3.24 Joint research projects will help in avoiding duplication of efforts and pooling of resources
for better outcomes and deliverables.
Further Recommendation
3.25 The Committee earnestly hopes that these 10 priority areas see the light of day at
an early date and do not remain bogged down in inter-departmental red tapism. The
Committee recommends that a seamless mechanism may be involved to ensure smooth
transformation of these 10 priority areas into actual implementation on the ground and
would like to be apprised of the specific steps undertaken/ being undertaken in this
direction.

AND NATURAL CALAMITIES

3.26 The Committee fails to see through the reasons for underperformance under the Scheme
of Establishment of Network of Laboratories of managing Epidemics and Natural Calamities. With
this pace of performance, the Committee does not understand how the target of establishing 10
Regional Labs, 30 State Level Labs and 120 Medical Colleges Labs, as envisaged during the
Twelfth Plan period would be achieved. Even funds could be released to only 4 Regional Labs, 5
State Level Labs and 16 Medical Colleges Labs out of the approved 5 Regional Labs, 11 State Level

13
Labs and 35 Medical College Labs. The Department needs to do some serious introspection to look
into the cause for not meeting the targets set. The Committee impresses upon the Department to
draw an action plan to meet the physical and financial targets set under the Scheme.
Action Taken

medical college level laboratories) have been approved.

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee is concerned to find that there were savings of significant magnitude under
several important heads during 2013-14 and 2014-15 as is evident from Table Nos. 2 and 3 given
above. The fact that the savings were not just the result of implementation of economy measures
but occurred due to various reasons like non-filing of posts, non-approval of schemes, delay in
execution work, slow space of construction etc., clearly suggests that there were inadequacies in
the monitoring mechanism, as well as budgetary planning process and budget allocations were
proposed without obtaining all necessary clearances. The Committee is of the firm view that the

INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION
Recommendation/Observation
2.40 The Committee observes that despite the above steps taken by the Ministry the overall
standard of education in AYUSH colleges continues to be poor. The Committee therefore
recommends the Ministry to reorient its focus on improving the quality and standards of A YUSH
education in the country and regulating the same effectively. The Committee would like the Ministry
to have the accreditation standards of AYUSH Colleges prescribed by the Quality Council of India.
 (Para 128)
Action Taken
2.41 A yurveda, Siddha and Unani (ASU) education and systems of medicine are regulated under
the provisions of the Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 1970 (IMCC Act) and the relevant
regulations made thereunder. The Central Council of Indian Medicine (CCIM) is a statutory body
made under the IMCC Act to regulate the practice and education of these ASU systems of
medicine. There is no provision in the IMCC Act and its Regulations to follow any standard of any
other Act and Regulations prescribed by any other Council except CCIM. Therefore, it will be in
violation of IMCC Act and its Regulations to have the accreditation standards of AYUSH Colleges
prescribed by the Quality Council of India.
2.42 It is pertinent to mention here that the CCIM is the only regulatory authority to prescribe
the standards of education and infrastructure of ASU Colleges by the way of notifications with the
prior approval of the Central Government. All the Gazette notifications of subordinate legislations
published by the CCIM are laid down on both the tables of Parliament (Rajya Sabha and Lok
Sabha) as per the provisions of the Act.  Hence, the Quality Council of India cannot prescribe the
standards of education and infrastructure of ASU Colleges and a college cannot follow the two
different standards at the same time.
2.43 The CCIM has made a number of Regulations to regulate the quality education in ASU
systems at undergraduate and postgraduate levels. The Council is revising from time to time the
course and curriculum of study in ASU Colleges as per the recommendations of the various
committees of the expert set up for the purpose. The suggestions from different forums, experts
and stake holders are also invited and incorporated in preparation and amendment of the Regulations
and curriculum. Any new Regulation or amendment is also circulated by the Council to all State
Governments for their comments before notification.  A list of CCIM’s Regulations and
amendments made so far to regulate and improve the quality education of Ayurveda, Siddha and
Unani (ASU) systems of medicine can be seen at Annexure-B.
2.44 Presently, there are 334 ASU Colleges with annual intake capacity of 21004 students (17628
UG + 3376 PG) (281 Ayurveda Colleges with 15087 under-graduate seats and 3089
post-graduate seats, 9 Siddha Colleges with 410 under-graduate seats and 140 post-graduate seats
and 44 Unani Colleges with 2131 under-graduate seats and 147 post-graduate seats).

QUALITY CONTROL OF ASU&H DRUGS
Recommendation/Observation
3.32 The Committee observes that quality control and standardization of ASU&H drugs leaves
much to be desired. It has often been reported in the media that Ayurveda and Homoeopathy drugs,
which were given to patients for various ailments, were laced with steroids and other improper
drugs. Permissible limits of heavy metals, pesticide residue, microbial load etc. are also sometimes
breached and regulatory needs of standardization and quality control of ASU&H drugs get seriously
impaired. On the issue of setting up of a separate Drug Controller of AYUSH, the decision to
develop a vertical structure of AYUSH in the present Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation
(CDSCO) headed by the Drug Controller General of India is not acceptable to the Committee. The
Committee feels that in order to strengthen regulatory mechanism and effectively oversee the
quality control of ASU&H drugs, setting up of a separate Central Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs
is an imminent necessity since a wing of AYUSH in the existing CDSCO may not produce the
desired result of effective regulation of ASU&H drugs. The Committee is of the view that a
separate Central Drugs Controller of AYUSH will help synergise the core competencies of the
Central and State Regulatory Authorities by developing dynamic relation between them and also go
a long way in building credibility in ASU&H drugs besides promoting AYUSH in foreign countries.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that action be initiated to set up an independent and
separate Central Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs at the earliest.  (Para 108)
Action Taken
3.33 The Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules thereunder provide licensing and enforcement
powers to the State Governments for Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homeopathic (ASU&H) drugs.
The Central Government makes and amends the legal provisions for ASU&H drugs, which are
enforced by the State Governments and support is provided for strengthening of enforcement
framework in the States.  The proposal of a separate Central Drugs Controller General of India
for AYUSH aimed at overseeing the implementation of regulatory provisions for ASU&H drugs in
the country was moved on the basis of recommendations of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Drugs
Consultative Committee since 2010.  The objective is to develop improved coordination between
Central and State Regulatory Authorities for quality control of ASU&H drugs and facilitate effective
supervision over enforcement of the provisions of Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Rules,
1945 pertaining to Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs. Recently, Government has
considered to set up a structured central regulatory regime for AYUSH medicines and the current
proposal is to have a vertical structure for AYUSH in the Central Drugs Standard Control
Organization (CDSCO). Government has initiated procedural steps for setting up the vertical
structure of AYUSH in the CDSCO and the need for creation of a separate Drugs Controller
General for AYUSH may be assessed subsequently, the time-frame for which cannot be specified
at this stage.   The draft Recruitment Rules for the posts agreed by the Department of Expenditure
are in the process of approval for onward transmission to Department of Health & Family Welfare.

CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES
The Committee is constrained to state that the action taken reply does not allay
the concerns expressed by the Committee regarding a proposal of the Government to do
away with the distinction between Special Category and Non-special Category  States as
it has not touched upon this issue.  The Ministry has simply chosen to state the existing
distinction between States for the purpose of disbursement of grant-in-aid which the
Committee is well aware of.  The Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to state
in unambiguous terms whether there is any proposal to do away with the existing
distinction between Special category and Non-special Category States.  (Para 3.5)
UPDATION OF CENTRAL REGISTERS OF  INDIAN MEDICINE AND HOMOEOPATHY
The Committee desires the Ministry to fast-track the work of digitization and
complete all formalities in the matter in a time-bound matter.  (Para 3.9)
NATIONAL INSTITUTES UNDER MINISTR Y OF AYUSH
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF AYURVEDA (NIA), JAIPUR
The Committee expects that the assurance given by the Ministry would be translated
into action and not remain mere platitudes.  The Committee finds that the issue has been
hanging fire since 2013-14 and has not been resolved with alacrity it deserves.  The
Committee would therefore like the Ministry to expeditiously finalise amendments to
Recruitment Rules within a given time-frame to ensure that senior faculty positions are
filled in the current financial year. (Para 3.12)
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF HOMOEOPATHY (NIH), KOLKATA
The Committee has already made an appropriate recommendation at para 3.12  The
same recommendation stands repeated here. (Para 3.15)

NORTH EASTERN INSTITUTE OF FOLK MEDICINE (NEIFM) P ASSISHAT ARUNACHAL
PRADESH

NEIAH and NEIFM and non-compliance beyond the deadline should attract penalty on the
contractor/concerned persons. (Para 3.20)
SCHEME FOR GRANT-IN-AID TO NON-PROFIT/NON-GOVERNMENTAL AYUSH
ORGANIZATIONS/INSTITUTIONS FOR UP-GRADATION TO CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE
The Committee is very much peeved to see that funds could not be utilized fully
during the year 2014-15 as sufficient numbers of new proposals were not received and the
ones received were incomplete/not as per the guidelines.  The Committee is of the view that
if the Ministry is providing funds for the new proposals but there are no takers for the

Scheme for Grant-in-Aid. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government
should review the structure of the Scheme and come up with necessary modifications and
also to look into the fact whether proper dissemination of the information in regard to the
Scheme to concerned agencies was ensured or not.  (Para 3.26)

within a given time-frame.  The C ommittee desires to be kept apprised of developments
in this regard. (Para 3.38)

Steps taken to regulate and improve the quality education of Ayurveda, Siddha and
Unani (ASU) systems of medicine
Amendment in the IMCC Act: To regulate and improve the quality and standards of
education and infrastructure in Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani (ASU) Medical Colleges, the Indian
Medicine Central Council Act was passed in 1970. The Act was amended  vide  the IMCC
(Amendment) Act, 2003. With effect to these amendments from 07.11.2003, the power to grant
the permission for establishment of new colleges, increase in admission capacity in any course
of study/training and starting a higher or new course of study/training and also to grant
permission to existing ASU colleges vests with the Central Government.
Regulations for new colleges, new courses and increase in seats: To grant permission for
establishment of new colleges, increase in admission capacity in any course of study/training
and starting a higher or new course of study/training the new Regulations made namely “The
Establishment of New Medical College, Opening of New or Higher Course of Study or Training
and Increase of Admission Capacity by a Medical College Regulations, 2003 read with
amendment Regulations of 2013”.
Regulations for existing ASU colleges: To grant permission to existing ASU colleges the new
Regulations made namely “The Indian Medicine Central Council (Permission to Existing Medical
Colleges) Regulations, 2006”.
Other UG/PG ASU Regulations:  To control, regulate and maintain the uniform standards of
quality education in Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani (ASU) Colleges and to produce adequate
manpower, following Regulations and their amendments have been notified from time to time:
i. PG Ayurveda Regulations: The Indian Medicine Central Council (Post-graduate
Ayurveda Education) Regulations, 2005 and amendments in 2012 made for nomen-
clature of PG degree in different specialties, duration of PG course, admission
criteria, method of training, examination & assessment, qualification of teaching
staff and minimum requirement for PG Ayurveda Colleges.
ii. PG Unani Regulations: The Indian Medicine Central Council (Post-graduate Unani
Education) Regulations, 2007 made for nomenclature of PG degree in different
specialties, duration of PG course, admission criteria, method of training, examina-
tion & assessment, qualification of teaching staff and minimum requirement for PG
Unani Colleges.
iii. MSR for Ayurveda colleges: The Indian Medicine Central Council (Minimum
Standard Requirements of Ayurveda Colleges and attached Hospitals) Regulations,
2012 and amended in 2013 for requirement of land, constructed area of college &
hospital, admission capacity, requirement of hospital including beds, no. of patients
in OPD/IPD, hospital staff, requirement of college including teaching/non-teaching
staff, phase-wise specific requirement of new colleges, requirement of equipment/
instruments, etc. for Ayurveda Colleges.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family
Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf present this Ninety-
second Report of the Committee on the Functioning of Medical Council of India (MCI).
2. The previous Committee had identified the subject ‘Medical  Council of India’ at its meeting held on
18th September, 2014. However, it could not conclude its examination of the subject. The present Committee
also took up the subject for detailed examination at is meeting held on 23rd September, 2015.
3. The Committee examined the subject, in its sittings held on 25th September, 2014,  28th January,
2015, 12th May, 2015, 25th May, 2015, 27th July, 2015, 6th October, 2015 and 1st March, 2016. During
the course of the examination it took oral evidences of representatives of the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare and experts on the subject.  The Committee also received written submissions from experts. The
Committee wishes to appreciate the  contribution made by various official witnesses/experts (Annexures I
and II) who richly deserve Committee’s encomia for sharing their perspectives and valuable views with the
Committee and suggesting remedies to the problems afflicting Medical Education and Practice in the country
through their evidences and written submissions. The Committee also benefited  from discussions with
certain stakeholders and representatives of the State Governments during its study visit to Tamil Nadu and
Karnataka from 8th June to 12th June, 2015 and local study visit to Vardhaman Mahavir Medical College
(VMMC), New Delhi and Shri Guru Govind Singh Tercentenary Medical College (SGGSTMC), Gurgaon on
the 2nd February, 2016.
4. The Committee had also invited views from various stakeholders in response to which 46 Memoranda
had been received (Annexure-III). The Memoranda were forwarded to the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare for comments which informed the Committee that the  same had been forwarded to the MCI which
has formed a Committee to examine the issues raised in the memoranda. The President, MCI informed that
the report is already prepared and has passed through EC (Executive Committee) and now will go to GB
(General Body) in March, 2016. On a direction by the Committee to expedite the said GB body meeting, the
President, MCI promised to expedite the same. Till the presentation of this report the comments have not
been received, and Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over such casual attitude of the Ministry and the
MCI.
5. During the finalization of its Report, the Committee relied upon the following documents/papers: ----
(i) Status Note on MCI received from Department of Health and Family W elfare;
(ii) Oral Evidence tendered by Secretary, Department of Health and Family W elfare alongwith the
President, MCI;
(iii) Oral Evidence tendered by Experts/Stakeholders;
(iv) W ritten submissions made by Experts/stakeholders; and
(v) Replies to the questionnaires received from the Department of Health and Family Welfare;

(v)

(vii) Articles published in various fora; and
(viii) Other relevant documents
6. The Committee considered the Draft Report and ad opted the same in its meeting held on 1st March,
2016.

have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report and also reproduced at the end of the Report in

REPORT
CHAPTER–I
BACKGROUND
1.1 Despite having the most number of medical colleges in the world, and currently having approximately
9.29 lakhs doctors enrolled on the Indian Medical Register, India is way behind in achieving the targeted
doctor population ratio of 1:1000 as per WHO norms. Shortage of doctors, who are the most important
cog in the health care delivery system, has derailed both access to and quality of health care, especially
to the vulnerable and poorer sections of the country.
1.2 Though there have been substantial improvements in health outcomes over the years, there are still
large gaps in health care accessibility in many parts of the country and Universal Health Care still remains
a distant dream. Issues concerning medical education, access to adequate health care to all people and
the entrenched inadequacy of health and clinical governance in the country have been engaging the
attention of the Committee for quite some time. The Committee has been given to understand that the
following issues have been widely debated in various fora across the country:
i. failure of the current system to produce doctors including specialists and super specialists
in adequate numbers and of requisite quality;
ii. deficiency of teachers in medical colleges;
iii. poor regulation of Undergraduate (UG) and Postgraduate (PG) education;
iv. disconnect between medical education system and health system;
v. opacity in the functioning of the existing regulatory body of medical education ( i.e. Medical
Council of India);
vi. lack of accountability of Medical Council of India (MCI);
vii. geographical mal-distribution of medical colleges;
viii. failure of the MCI in discharging its mandated responsibilities;
ix. allegations of rampant corruption in the MCI;
x. constitution and composition of the MCI;
xi. absence of proper screening and admission procedures in private medical colleges;
xii. need for common entrance test for admissions to MBBS,Postgraduate and Super-specialty
medical courses;
xiii. prevalence of capitation fee in private medical colleges in flagrant violation of the law;
xiv. barriers to expansion of medical education;
xv. lack of a robust accreditation system for UG and PG Medical education;

2
xvi. gross inequity between rural and urban India in terms of availability of health care services;
xvii. ethical issues;
xviii. need for reforms in the regulatory framework of medical education and practice;
xix. over-investigation and over-treatment in private hospitals;
xx. inadequacy of self-regulatory processes for medical profession.
1.3 Since the Medical Council of India is mandated to play a pivotal role in regulating medical
education and practice in the country, the Committee decided to holistically examine its role and functioning
with the ultimate aim of suggesting veritable solutions to the inadequacies that are currently plaguing our
medical education and health care delivery systems.
1.4 At the initial stage of examination of the subject, the Committee called for a background note on
the functioning of Medical Council of India (MCI) from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Background of MCI furnished by Ministry
1.5 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in the background note submitted to the Committee
stated that the Medical Council of India was established in 1934 under the Indian Medical Council Act,
1933, with the main function of establishing uniform standards of higher qualifications in medicine and
recognition of medical qualifications in India and abroad. The Act was repealed and replaced by a new
Act in 1956. The Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 was further amended in 1964, 1993, 2001.

The major reforms needed:
(viii) The Ministry in the background note, submitted to the Committee, indicated that the following

(a) There is need to restructure the MCI. The model favoured is that of a lean and professional
